La partie liquide du Fonds de la richesse nationale s’épuiserait rapidement, au rythme des ponctions actuelles (environ 400 milliards par trimestre). Le réarmement européen prendrait de l’ampleur (de l’ordre de 50 à 60 milliards de dollars d’ici à 2027) et Trump, entièrement absorbé par les élections de mi-mandat, pourrait perdre tout intérêt pour un quelconque « accord ». La stratégie optimale consisterait à obtenir le maximum par voie diplomatique tout en maintenant en parallèle une pression militaire constante – non pas l’une ou l’autre option, mais les deux à la fois. 2. Le temps est un allié précieux, mais pas indéfiniment. Au rythme de dépenses actuel, la partie liquide du Fonds de la richesse nationale pourrait être épuisée dès fin 2026 ou début 2027. L’alternative serait un recours accru aux obligations d’État (avec une dette publique s’élevant déjà à 31 300 milliards de roubles en mars 2026). Avec un taux directeur de 15 %, le coût du service de la dette dépasserait cependant 15 % du budget. Le multiplicateur militaire de 1,5x ne compenserait pas la contraction du secteur civil pendant plus de deux ans. La baisse simultanée du crédit immobilier, du secteur de la construction et de la croissance du crédit constituent autant de signes d’une stagnation de l’arrière civil, qui sape les fondements mêmes de l’effort de guerre russe. Les recettes pétrogazières ont chuté de 45,4 % au premier trimestre 2026 en tombant à 1 440 milliards de roubles et le budget ne parvient pas à s’équilibrer. L’abaissement du taux directeur à 12-13 % avant la fin 2026 (selon la prévision de Sberbank) offrirait un répit au secteur civil, mais la pression inflationniste pourrait lui faire obstacle en cas de guerre prolongée. 3. La protection de l’arrière est une condition sine qua non dans tout cas de figure Aucun avantage stratégique ne saurait être atteint sans aborder de front le problème de la défense anti-aérienne à l’arrière. Le Flamingo ukrainien (FP-5) frappe à plus de 1 500 km, avec une coque composite qui complique sa détection ; en parallèle, le FP-7 balistique (200-300 km, 1 500 m/s) et le FP-9 (850 km) poursuivent leur développement. Les drones FPV, dont la portée a maintenant triplé (150 km), effectuent des frappes en profondeur sur des installations autrefois jugées sûres. Entre 10 et 15 % des capacités de raffinage sont endommagées et jusqu’à 35 % des composants de défense anti-aérienne ont été perdus. Au niveau de la vie économique à l’arrière, le taux directeur de 15 % étouffe le secteur civil. Les investissements sont entravés, la construction recule dans tous les domaines, les petites entreprises empruntent à plus de 20 %. La pénurie de main-d’œuvre dans les entreprises de défense (entre 80 000 et 400 000 personnes) limite la montée en puissance de la production. Trois goulots d’étranglement critiques méritent une attention particulière : la microélectronique (sans composants occidentaux, les armes de précision présentent des surcoûts conséquents), les munitions (le facteur limitant étant ici d’ordre humain, non financier, avec un premier recul de production observé en septembre 2025) et enfin les moteurs (où tous les producteurs, de l’aviation à la marine en passant par les missiles, sont en surcharge). 4. Un facteur potentiellement décisif : la supériorité technologique Le premier camp capable de mettre en opération des essaims de drones entièrement autonomes (des milliers d’unités coordonnées par IA, sans opérateurs) à l’échelle d’une division obtiendrait un avantage tactique déterminant. Dans ce domaine, la Russie enregistre des succès industriels (7 à 9 millions de drones FPV, drone Lancet autonome et drones à fibre optique), tandis que l’Ukraine met l’accent sur la prédominance qualitative (navigation indépendante du GPS, guidage par apprentissage automatique, résistance au brouillage, logiciels d’IA occidentaux). L’écart tend néanmoins à se resserrer, confirmant que les investissements dans l’intelligence artificielle à usage militaire constituent une priorité stratégique. Le missile Tsirkon est désormais d’un usage courant et massif, avec autant de tirs au cours du seul mois de février 2026 qu’à l’échelle des deux années précédentes réunies. L’Ukraine répond à ces frappes en développant ses propres systèmes longue portée et en négociant l’acquisition de SAMP/T de nouvelle génération auprès de la France. 5. L’issue la plus probable n’est pas une « victoire », mais le « meilleur » scénario parmi ceux disponibles. Les scénarios 3 et 4 (le Trump deal et le « gel » de la situation sur le modèle coréen) totalisent à eux seuls 54 % de l’espace des probabilités. La préparation aux négociations représente donc une tâche au moins aussi vitale que la pression militaire elle-même. Les volets diplomatique et militaire doivent fonctionner non pas en alternance, mais de concert. 6. Le piège des coûts irrécupérables représente une menace cognitive bien réelle. Selon la Prospect Theory de Kahneman, les acteurs tendent à prendre davantage de risques en cas de perte ; or les deux parties en présence enregistrent des pertes lourdes : des centaines de milliers de pertes, une diplomatie en ruine, une pression considérable sur les économies. Les conclusions d’un calcul purement rationnel aboutiraient à prendre acte de ces pertes, mais l’aversion aux pertes ( loss aversion ) favorise au contraire la logique : « Poussons encore un peu et tous ces sacrifices seront compensés ». D’où la nécessité d’un mécanisme d’évaluation objective, indépendant des inerties de la politique du jour. 7. La trêve pascale du 11-12 avril est un signal à prendre en compte. Le 9 avril, Poutine a annoncé une trêve unilatérale de 32 heures, du 11 avril à 16 heures jusqu’à la fin du 12 avril. Zelensky a accepté en réponse des « mesures symétriques ». Si la trêve est respectée par les deux camps, la probabilité du volet diplomatique augmente, renforçant d’autant le troisième scénario ; en revanche, en cas de rupture, les quatrième et cinquième scénarios gagnent en probabilité. Le ministère russe de la Défense a ordonné à ses troupes de rester en alerte face à d’éventuelles provocations, ce qui confirme bien qu’il s’agit moins d’une trêve de confiance que d’un test. L’article Les huit scénarios de la guerre en Ukraine (texte intégral de la note Sberbank) est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: Washington sanctionne, Akane riposte: la CPI défend son indépendance
items.description: La présidente de la Cour pénale internationale (CPI), Tomoko Akane, a vigoureusement rejeté, le mercredi 26 août 2026, les accusations portées par Washington contre la juridiction et sa direction. Visée par des sanctions américaines annoncées le 18 août dernier, la magistrate japonaise dénonce une campagne de pression destinée, selon elle, à fragiliser l’indépendance de la Cour, rapportent des médias. La présidente de la CPI ne compte visiblement pas rester silencieuse face aux sanctions américaines. Mercredi 26 août 2026, Tomoko Akane a réfuté les accusations formulées par les États-Unis à l’encontre de la juridiction internationale, après l’adoption de mesures visant plusieurs de ses responsables. Le Département d’État américain avait annoncé, le mardi 18 août, des sanctions contre Tomoko Akane, de nationalité japonaise, ainsi que contre Abdoulaye Seye, avocat principal de la CPI et ressortissant sénégalais. Ces mesures prévoient notamment le «gel de leurs avoirs détenus aux États-Unis ou transitant par le système financier américain». Face à ces accusations, la présidente de la Cour se veut catégorique. «Il n’y a tout simplement aucun fondement» aux reproches américains, a-t-elle déclaré, rejetant notamment les allégations selon lesquelles la CPI serait une organisation politique corrompue ou aurait détourné le droit international pour porter atteinte à la souveraineté des États. Neuf juges dans le viseur de Washington La pression américaine touche désormais une partie importante des instances dirigeantes de la CPI. Selon la juridiction, l’administration du président Donald Trump a sanctionné neuf des dix-huit juges de la Cour, ainsi que deux procureurs adjoints, l’ancien procureur général et un autre membre du bureau du procureur. Washington reproche principalement à la CPI d’avoir outrepassé ses prérogatives en enquêtant sur des responsables politiques et militaires des pays qui ne sont pas parties au Statut de Rome, notamment les États-Unis et Israël. Tomoko Akane rejette cependant toute justification à son encontre. Elle a assuré n’avoir «absolument aucune raison» d’être sanctionnée, considérant les mesures américaines comme une nouvelle étape d’une campagne de pression plus large contre la juridiction. Akane sollicite l’appui de Tokyo Dans ce contexte tendu, la présidente de la CPI a appelé le Japon à jouer un rôle auprès de son allié américain afin d’éviter une nouvelle escalade. Elle a également exhorté Tokyo à travailler avec les autres États membres de la Cour pour qu’ils ne cèdent pas aux pressions américaines et ne renoncent pas à leur appartenance à la CPI. À travers cette riposte, Tomoko Akane entend défendre non seulement son institution, mais aussi le principe de son indépendance. Alors que les sanctions américaines frappent désormais une part importante des responsables de la Cour, le bras de fer entre Washington et la CPI semble appelé à se poursuivre. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article Washington sanctionne, Akane riposte: la CPI défend son indépendance est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: ‘No Supreme Court seat is vacant’ — Afenyo-Markin objects to rushed Supreme Court nominees’ vetting
items.description: Minority Leader in Parliament, Alexander Afenyo-Markin, has challenged the urgency surrounding the proposed vetting of three nominees for appointment to the Supreme Court, arguing that there is currently no vacancy on the apex court to justify what he described as a compressed parliamentary timetable. Mr Afenyo-Markin objected on Thursday, August 27, 2026, when the Appointments Committee began the vetting of the three nominees nominated by President John Dramani Mahama. He stressed that the Minority’s position should not be interpreted as opposition to either the nominees or the President’s constitutional authority to make appointments to the Supreme Court. Rather, he said the objection was directed at the procedure and the speed with which Parliament was being asked to consider the nominations. “This is not an objection to the principle of vetting. It is an objection to the nominee; neither is it an objection to the nominees as individuals. It is an objection grounded in the Constitution, the 1992 Constitution and the standing orders of Parliament,” he said. ‘No vacancy, no urgency’ At the heart of the Minority’s objection, Mr Afenyo-Markin said, was the absence of a vacant seat on the Supreme Court. “We advance nine grounds. Each stands independently. Together they are, in our respectful submission conclusive: one, ground one, that there is no vacancy and therefore no exigency capable of justifying a compressed timetable,” he said. “Chairman, the Supreme Court of Ghana presently sits with its full complement of justices. No seat on the bench is vacant.” According to him, the three nominees were being considered as additions to the existing membership of the court rather than replacements necessitated by the death, retirement or removal of serving justices. “The three persons before this committee are nominated to add to the existing membership of the court, not to fill any gap left by death, retirement or removal,” he stated. He argued that the distinction was important because the justification for accelerating the process appeared to be based on urgency. “This matters because the entire justification offered for compressing the ordinary voting timetable is urgency. Urgency requires an urgent state of affairs where no vacancy exists,” he said. Mr Afenyo-Markin therefore challenged the Majority to demonstrate the specific consequences of delaying the appointments and subjecting the nominees to what he described as the normal scrutiny associated with Supreme Court appointments. “The committee is respectfully urged to require the majority to identify precisely and on record what harm befalls a state, the judiciary, or any litigant if these three additional appointments are averted with the same care that would ordinarily attend any Supreme Court nomination,” he said. “We submit that no such harm can be shown because none exists.” Three-day timetable questioned The Minority Leader also questioned the decision to complete the process within a period he said left only three sitting days for Parliament to consider the matter. He maintained that the accelerated process was inconsistent with the established practice for Supreme Court nominations since the adoption of the 1992 Constitution. “We submit that since 1992, all Supreme Court nominees have gone through the regular period of notice where this committee advertises in the dailies for two weeks,” he said. He further questioned whether the mere announcement of the President’s nominations in Parliament should trigger an immediate vetting and voting process within a matter of days. “It must not be that just Monday when Mr. Speaker announced the nomination as received from the President, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday, Parliament is supposed to vote,” he said. Mr Afenyo-Markin emphasised that the Minority was not questioning President Mahama’s constitutional mandate to nominate persons for appointment to the Supreme Court. “It is not our position that we are against any of the nominees. Neither are we saying that the President doesn’t have the constitutional mandate to nominate for Supreme Court,” he said. Minority seeks objection on record The Minority Leader said the formal objection was intended to ensure that Parliament dealt with the procedural concerns before proceeding further with the vetting. He said the objection should be recorded regardless of the eventual decision of the committee. “We ask that this objection be resolved before this committee to proceed further and that it appear on the record of these proceedings, regardless of how it is resolved,” he stated. The development sets the stage for a potentially contentious debate over the balance between the President’s power to nominate Supreme Court justices, Parliament’s oversight responsibilities and the procedures governing the consideration of such nominations. For the Minority, however, the central question remains whether there is sufficient urgency to depart from what Mr Afenyo-Markin described as the established process for considering appointments to Ghana’s highest court.

items.title: Bosnian Serb commander and war criminal Ratko Mladic dies in prison

items.title: PTI to hold rally in Karachi on Sept 6, KP CM Sohail Afridi to tour Sindh
items.description: KARACHI: The PTI on Thursday announced that it would hold a public rally on Shahrah-i-Quaideen in Karachi on Sept 6, while Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi is scheduled to begin a four-day visit to Sindh on Sept 3 along with the party’s central leadership. Addressing a press conference in Karachi, PTI Sindh President Haleem Adil Sheikh said Afridi and the party’s central leadership would enter Sindh on Sept 3. The delegation would receive a major welcome at Kamoon Shaheed at 11am before travelling to different cities across the province, he said. “The delegation, led by CM Afridi, will travel from Jacobabad to Naushehro Feroze on Sept 4, proceed from Naushehro Feroze to Hyderabad on Sept 5 and reach Karachi on Sept 6,” he announced. Sheikh added that large gatherings linked to the party’s street movement would also be held in different cities during the tour. “A major rally will be held on Shahrah-i-Quaideen in Karachi on Sept 6,” Sheikh said, expressing hope that the authorities would grant permission for the event. “Even if permission is not granted, there will be a rally in Karachi,” he asserted. He said Sept 6 was Defence Day and that the PTI would speak about the defence of Pakistan and the rights of its people. Speaking at the same press conference, PTI Secretary General Salman Akram Raja said the PTI would also observe Sept 27 as Democracy Day and protest for the release of party founder Imran Khan, and called on people to continue raising their voices for their rights. “This is not a battle for one day; it is a question of the future of the entire nation,” he said. Raja said the country’s poor had expressed themselves through their votes, but their mandate had been “stolen”. He claimed millions of Pakistanis had voted for Imran on Feb 8, 2024, in the hope of determining their future, but their mandate was subsequently denied. He also claimed that PTI candidates had won 21 of the 22 National Assembly seats in Karachi, while seats won by the party in Lahore and elsewhere had also been “taken away”. Referring to reports of electoral irregularities, he alleged that the elections were marred by “worst rigging” and that candidates rejected by voters were subsequently imposed on them. PTI Secretary General Raja said Pakistan had effectively developed two separate systems — one for the rich and another for the poor — and that the deaths of 14 newborn babies at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) had exposed the failure of a system that did not adequately protect the disadvantaged. Expressing grief over the infants’ deaths, Raja said the tragedy had raised serious questions about the state of public healthcare. “A committee comprising those responsible has been formed, but the question is: where is the country heading?” he said. He warned that a tragedy of this nature could occur anywhere in the country. Referring to claims that “the system had failed”, he asked which system had actually failed. “We need to fix the system that supports the poor,” he said. Raja also said around 25 million children in Pakistan were currently out of school and that the country was wasting their potential. “Poor children are not receiving the education they deserve,” he said, adding that Pakistan had developed a degree of social and educational segregation rarely seen elsewhere, including Bangladesh. “Pims tragedy is another manifestation of this inequality, as wealthy families generally do not depend on basic health units while poor people have no alternative,” he said. Raja claimed that around 40 per cent of children in the country were behind in mental development for their age, leaving them disadvantaged throughout their lives. “Imran Khan’s message is about the poor. He talks about equal education and opportunities for children of the rich and poor,” he said. The PTI leader also alleged that people who raised their voices were being picked up, while journalists who spoke the truth were being removed from their organisations. “Journalists who used to raise their voice for the truth are unemployed today,” he said. He said democracy had never been allowed to fully flourish in Pakistan and questioned whether the creation of new provinces would resolve the country’s political problems. Islamabad, he noted, was a small city, yet its hospitals and education system were also facing serious difficulties. Raja further said any decision to create new provinces or alter the existing provincial structure should be taken by the people through an assembly representing their genuine mandate. He called for strengthening the local government system and devolving powers to the grassroots. “Everyone knows how the mayor was made in Karachi,” he said, adding that no system could function if people continued to be deprived of their electoral rights. Raja also alleged that PTI’s votes had been “stolen” in Karachi’s local government elections. He urged people to come out and make their voices heard, assuring them that the PTI leadership would remain at the forefront of the struggle. “If 250 million people come out of their homes and onto the streets, this system will collapse,” he said.

items.title: Tchad : destruction d’un stock important des médicaments de qualité douteuse
items.description: © (DR) Le ministère de la santé publique et de la prévention, à travers sa direction générale de la pharmacie, du médicament et des laboratoires, a lancé le mercredi 26 août 2026, sur le site de Gassi, l'opération de destruction d'un important stock de médicaments de qualité inférieure et falsifiés (MQIF). Cette opération, fait savoir le département, est l'aboutissement d'un travail d'équipe, rigoureux et exemplaire, de la commission nationale de lutte contre les médicaments de qualité inférieur et falsifiés. Le vice-président de la commission nationale de lutte contre les médicaments de qualité inférieur et falsifiés, Colonel Ibrahim Adoum Kaoussa, a précisé que la destruction des faux médicaments, d’origines douteuses saisis lors des contrôles menés par ladite commission, permet de s'assurer qu'aucun médicament dangereux ne circule plus sur le marché. Les conclusions de cette expertise ont confirmé que ces produits pharmaceutiques sont contrefaits, non homologués, d’origine douteuse, interdits et dépourvus de toute traçabilité et introduits sur le territoire national sans aucune autorisation d’importation. Il a rappelé qu’avec les médicaments de la rue et les contrefaçons ne sont pas des soins mais constituent un poison. Ils représentent une menace directe, grave et inacceptable pour la vie et la santé des concitoyens. Face au caractère toxique de ces substances et de prévenir tout risque de réintroduction clandestine ou de fuite vers le marché, le ministère de la santé publique et de la prévention applique la tolérance zéro. L’article Tchad : destruction d'un stock important des médicaments de qualité douteuse est apparu en premier sur Journal du Tchad .

items.title: NAPTIP accuses workers of attempting to traffic employer’s toddler in Cross River
items.description: The National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons (NAPTIP) has accused three workers in Ogoja, Cross River, of attempting to traffic their employer’s two-year-old child for sale. Mr Oba Joseph, Head of Operations, NAPTIP Cross River Command, told the News Agency of Nigeria in an interview on Thursday in Calabar. Joseph ‌said the agency received a call on Monday about the incident, which occurred in Ogberia Ochoro community, in which three suspects allegedly took a two-year-old child while attempting to move him to another location for sale. According to him, the suspects claimed they had worked for their employer for about three months without receiving their wages. “They claimed they decided to traffic the child as revenge and to recover the money they said they were owed.” The NAPTIP boss, however, said the employer disputed the allegation of owing the workers, insisting he had paid them, except for August, which had not ended. He noted that the suspects were apprehended after a farmer returning from the farm noticed their suspicious movement with the child. “The farmer questioned them, after which one of the suspects allegedly claimed that the two-year-old child was his own. “The farmer, who was not satisfied with their explanation, raised an alarm, leading to the suspects’ arrest after they had crossed about four communities,” he narrated. Joseph said investigations were ongoing, adding that the agency would prosecute the suspects after concluding its investigation. He said a major issue was the disparity in the suspects’ ages, with the community documenting them as 18, 19 and 27. The suspects, however, told NAPTIP they were 16, 17 and 25, prompting the agency to seek their parents’ assistance to establish their actual ages. Joseph said if their ages were confirmed as stated, they could be treated as children in conflict with the law, potentially affecting how the court handles the case. He stressed, however, that regardless of their ages, the attempted trafficking of the two-year-old child remained established, while the investigation would determine the appropriate prosecution process. The post NAPTIP accuses workers of attempting to traffic employer’s toddler in Cross River appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: CDF Munir, Kuwaiti delegation vow to strengthen 'mutually beneficial defence partnership'
items.description: Pakistan and Kuwait reaffirmed the resolve to “consolidate their historic and brotherly relations into a strong, enduring and mutually beneficial defence partnership”, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said on Thursday. A Kuwaiti delegation led by Defence Minister Sheikh Abdullah Ali Abdullah Al-Saleem Al-Sabah met Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir at General Headquarters (GHQ) in Rawalpindi, ISPR said in a statement . The Kuwaiti minister was accompanied by Chief of General Staff of the Armed Forces Lt Gen Khaled Darj Saad Al-Shriaan. The two sides discussed “matters of mutual interest, regional security and bilateral defence cooperation”, ISPR said. “Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to enhancing institutional ties and expanding mutually beneficial defence collaboration between the two brotherly countries.” ISPR added that “the Kuwaiti delegation appreciated the professionalism, operational excellence and valuable contributions of the Pakistan Armed Forces towards regional peace and stability”. The two sides discussed contributing to regional security and stability as well. Pakistan and Kuwait also signed ‘Protocol Agreement 2026’, “significantly expanding bilateral military cooperation” under their 2023 Defence Cooperation Agreement, state-run Pakistan TV reported. The pact was signed during a meeting between the Kuwait defence minister and his Pakistani counterpart Khawaja Asif in Rawalpindi. “Pakistan’s Armed Forces will assist Kuwait in training, capacity building, border management and other mutually agreed areas of defence cooperation,” Pakistan TV added. The signing comes about a month after Kuwait ratified the 2023 agreement with Pakistan. Days after the ratification, Kuwaiti Foreign Minister Sheikh Jarrah Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah paid an official visit to Pakistan, where he met CDF Munir and discussed matters of mutual interest and regional security. Sheikh Jarrah had expressed appreciation for Pakistan’s steadfast support and constructive contribution toward regional peace and stability. During his visit, which was the first by a Kuwaiti foreign minister in more than five years, Sheikh Jarrah also called on Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and his Pakistani counterpart Ishaq Dar. There’s been a noticeable uptick in high-level contacts between the two countries over the past few mon­ths, including exchanges between senior military officials and discussions on expanding defence cooperation, as Kuwait broadened its security partnerships amid continuing volatility across the Gulf.

items.title: Le Cameroun recherche 150 milliards de F pour construire un pipeline et un dépôt pétrolier à Kribi
items.description: © DR Une rencontre entre les porteurs de projet et les investisseurs a eu lieu le 26 août dernier à Douala avec pour ambition de faire avancer le projet. Pour doter la ville portuaire de Kribi d'un dépôt pétrolier et d'un pipeline, le Cameroun se lance à la recherche des partenaires pouvant financer le projet. C'est dans cette optique que la Société camerounaise des dépôts pétroliers a organisé mercredi une rencontre avec les investisseurs et financiers. Le but de la rencontre est de mobiliser les fonds en vue de la construction dudit dépôt pétrolier. Le coût du projet est évalué à 150 milliards de francs CFA. En vue de mobiliser ces fonds, les démarches sont menées par des cabinets PG & Partners ainsi que la banque ivoirienne Matha Capital. Bien engagé en vue de la réalisation de ce projet, le Cameroun a déjà posé certains actes dont la création d'une ligne dans la structure des prix des produits pétroliers en perspective du financement. L'autre action dans ce sens est la mise en place le 17 août dernier des organes sociaux du dépôt pétrolier de Kribi. À la direction du dépôt pétrolier se trouve Patrice Entame Etame, tandis que Véronique Moampea Mbio, directrice générale de la SCDP, assure la présidence du conseil d'administration. Les financements recherchés permettront de réaliser un projet qui contribuera à réduire la dépendance au Port de Douala, d'accueillir des navires plus grands, d'accélérer le changement et réduire les délais de traitement, renforcer le stockage national, peut-on lire dans une publication de la SCDP en date du 26 août 2026. La rencontre de mercredi s'est tenue à la suite de l'inauguration le 21 août dernier à Douala de trois nouvelles infrastructures dont une nouvelle sphère à gaz domestique à Bonaberi, un nouveau pipeline et un nouveau siège pour la SCDP. La structure est ainsi dans la dynamique de d'améliorer l'approvisionnement en gaz et en carburants au Cameroun dans un contexte où des signaux de pénuries sont d temps en temps donnes à travers la rareté du gaz domestique ou encore du pétrole lampant. Cet article Le Cameroun recherche 150 milliards de F pour construire un pipeline et un dépôt pétrolier à Kribi est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Carburants | Menace de grève des transporteurs pour les 23 et 24 septembre
items.description: Comme si, en pleine canicule estivale, les coupures fréquentes d’électricité et d’eau du robinet, les pénuries d’eau embouteillée, les longs retards des vols de la compagnie nationale Tunisair, entre autres désagréments, ne suffisaient pas au malheur des Tunisiens, voilà que l’on annonce, pour très bientôt, de longues files d’attente devant les stations d’essence pour remplir les réservoirs des voitures. Le département du secteur privé de l'Union générale tunisienne du travail (UGTT) a émis, ce jeudi 27 août 2026, un préavis de grève pour le secteur du transport d'hydrocarbures, annonçant une grève sectorielle les 23 et 24 septembre 2026 sur tous les lieux de travail à travers le territoire national. Les représentants des travailleurs du secteur, réunis hier mercredi au siège de l'UGTT sous la supervision du secrétaire général adjoint chargé du secteur privé et du secrétaire général de la Fédération générale du pétrole et des produits chimiques, ont justifié cette grève par le non-respect, par les parties administratives, de l’application des accords antérieurs, notamment celui conclu le 2 mai 2019,ainsi que des obligations légales, principalement la couverture sociale auprès de la Caisse nationale de sécurité sociale (CNSS), indique le préavis de grève, dont une copie a été adressée aux ministres des Affaires sociales, de l’Industrie, des Mines et de l’Énergie, de l’Intérieur, du Commerce et du Développement des exportations, ainsi qu’au ministre du Transport, au directeur des conflits du travail et de la promotion des relations professionnelles, au président de l'Union tunisienne de l’industrie, du commerce et de l’artisanat (Utica), au président de la Chambre nationale du transport de matières dangereuses (relevant de l’Utica) et aux représentants légaux des entreprises de transport de marchandises et d’hydrocarbures, précise encore le préavis de grève. Si, donc, d’ici le 23 mai, rien ne serait fait pour régler ce problème, c’est que personne, parmi tous ces responsables, ne se soucie de soulager les Tunisiens des maux qui les accablent. I. B. L’article Carburants | Menace de grève des transporteurs pour les 23 et 24 septembre est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Motorists lament obstruction, accident trap on Enugu-Onitsha Expressway
items.description: By Chinedu Adonu ENUGU — Motorists plying the Enugu-Onitsha Expressway have raised the alarm over an abandoned heavy-duty truck obstructing the highway at 9th Mile Corner, describing the situation as a death trap for road users. The truck, which reportedly broke down about five days ago, has allegedly remained on the expressway, causing traffic congestion and contributing to multiple accidents in the area. The incident occurred near the site of the international motor parts market being constructed by the Enugu State Government. A motorist, Mr Uchenna Eze, who spoke to Vanguard on Wednesday evening, said the abandoned truck had contributed to several accidents, leaving some road users injured. He also said the obstruction had caused serious gridlock along the busy highway. Eze appealed to the Federal Road Safety Corps, FRSC, and the Enugu State Government to urgently remove the truck and restore the free flow of traffic. “This is a very bad situation. The place where the truck broke down is very dangerous and it has been causing accidents. “Today, being Wednesday, there was a multiple accident and a lot of people were injured and taken to the hospital for treatment,” he said. According to him, the continued presence of the truck was particularly concerning because an FRSC checkpoint was located close to the area. “The FRSC mounts a road checkpoint close to here, and I don’t know why they have not enforced the removal of the truck from the expressway to allow free flow of traffic. “They should urgently remove the truck to save the lives of travellers using this road,” Eze said. Efforts to obtain the reaction of the FRSC as of the time of filing this report were unsuccessful. The post Motorists lament obstruction, accident trap on Enugu-Onitsha Expressway appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Who’s Millicent Amankwah Yeboah, the 34-year-old first time MP married to Mahama Ayariga?
items.description: At 34, Millicent Amankwah Yeboah has already established a place for herself in Ghana’s political space, serving as the Member of Parliament for Sunyani West in the Ninth Parliament. But beyond her role as a legislator, Mrs Amankwah Yeboah is also the wife of Majority Leader Mahama Ayariga, a detail that came into the spotlight during her husband’s vetting by Parliament’s Appointments Committee on Thursday, August 27, 2026. The brief exchange offered an opportunity for many Ghanaians to take a closer look at the young legislator, who represents the National Democratic Congress (NDC) in Parliament. From business to Parliament Mrs Amankwah Yeboah entered Parliament after winning the Sunyani West seat in the December 2024 general election. She defeated the then-incumbent New Patriotic Party (NPP) MP, Ignatius Baffour-Awuah, to become the representative of the constituency in the Ninth Parliament. In the 2024 election, she beat Ignatius Baffour Awuah by securing 26,828 votes, representing 57.64% of the total valid votes cast. The NPP’s candidate polled 19,715 votes, representing 42.36%, whereas the PNC’s Adongo Matilda polled zero votes. Her entry into Parliament marked a transition from a career in business management and consultancy to national politics. Before becoming an MP, she served as a branch manager for Verna Mineral Water and later as Managing Director of MEA Connect Consultants. Her academic background includes studies at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) in Ghana and the University of Law in the United Kingdom. Finding her feet in Parliament As a first-term legislator, Mrs Amankwah Yeboah has taken on parliamentary responsibilities beyond representing her constituents. She serves on committees of Parliament, including the Employment, Labour Relations and Pensions Committee, where she contributes to discussions on issues relating to employment and labour. Her political journey also places her in an unusual position in Ghana’s parliamentary history, serving in the same Parliament as her husband. Mahama Ayariga, the MP for Bawku Central, was the Majority Leader until his recent reassignment to the Ministry of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, and is a veteran legislator who has held several political and ministerial positions. The couple’s presence in Parliament means they are not only partners at home but also colleagues within Ghana’s legislature. The moment that brought her into the spotlight Mrs Amankwah Yeboah attracted wider public attention on Thursday when she accompanied her husband to his ministerial vetting. As the Appointments Committee Chairman, Bernard Ahiafor, introduced members of Mr Ayariga’s family who were present, he mentioned his father-in-law but initially did not identify his wife. Mr Ayariga quickly pointed out the omission. “Mr Chairman, you have introduced the father-in-law, but you haven’t introduced the daughter,” he said. Mr Ahiafor then introduced her as “Hon Mrs Ayariga, formerly known as Hon Millicent Yeboah-Amankwah”, identifying her as the Sunyani West MP. Read Also: Surprise at vetting as Mahama Ayariga reveals Sunyani West MP is his wife The light-hearted moment placed the young legislator briefly at the centre of attention, not because of a parliamentary debate or political controversy, but because of her connection to another prominent figure in the House. Yet her own political journey stands independently. At 34, Millicent Amankwah Yeboah represents a new generation of legislators navigating Ghana’s political landscape while combining parliamentary responsibilities with a career that began outside politics. Her story is therefore not simply that of the wife of a senior politician, but of a young woman who successfully contested and won a parliamentary seat and is now building her own record in Ghana’s legislature.

items.title: Burkina Faso : L’ONASSIM et l’ONBAH arment leurs agents de valeurs patriotiques au CNEC de Pô
items.description: L’Office national de sécurisation des sites miniers et des carrières (ONASSIM) a clôturé, le 26 août 2026 au Centre national d’entraînement commando (CNEC) de Pô, l’immersion patriotique de son personnel. Ce stage a été organisé conjointement avec l’Office national des barrages et aménagements hydro-agricoles (ONBAH). Accueillis au CNEC le 14 août 2026, les 115 agents des deux offices ont été soumis à un programme intensif combinant formation civique, patriotique et militaire, activités physiques, instruction au maniement des armes et techniques d’intervention. Le représentant du directeur du stage, le Capitaine Kagambega Romaric, a indiqué que cette immersion avait notamment pour objectif de renforcer chez les participants le respect des lois et des institutions, la responsabilité, la solidarité, la loyauté envers la nation, l’amour de la patrie et le sens du sacrifice. Au-delà des enseignements théoriques, les immergés ont été confrontés à des exercices destinés à éprouver leur endurance et leur capacité à dépasser leurs limites. Ils ont notamment appris à démonter et remonter des armes et ont participé à des séances de sport et d’instruction pratique. Selon le Capitaine Kagambega Romaric, les participants ont fait preuve d’assiduité, de discipline et d’esprit d’équipe durant leur séjour au CNEC. Les objectifs de l’immersion ont ainsi été jugés atteints par les cadres chargés de leur encadrement. À l’ONASSIM, les agents encouragés à être davantage patriotes-©Faso7 Pour les premiers responsables de l’ONASSIM, cette immersion doit surtout produire des effets au-delà du cadre du CNEC. Le chef d’escadron Arnold Ouédraogo, directeur général de l’office, a expliqué que l’initiative visait à former des agents davantage engagés au service de la Nation. « Notre motivation principale, c'est de former des agents engagés et davantage au service de la nation » , a-t-il souligné. La discipline, le patriotisme, le sens du devoir et le don de soi constituent, selon lui, les principales valeurs que l’office entend renforcer à travers cette expérience. Le directeur général attend désormais des agents qu’ils traduisent ces acquis dans leurs tâches quotidiennes. Il les appelle notamment à se débarrasser de certaines mauvaises habitudes et à faire preuve de plus de dévouement et de disponibilité dans l’accomplissement de leurs missions. « Une fois de retour, nous attendons que nos agents se débarrassent des tares d'avant, que les agents soient plus dévoués dans leurs tâches quotidiennes, que ces agents aient un sens plus élevé du patriotisme, le don de soi et surtout que ces agents acceptent de consentir à des sacrifices pour que les choses puissent bien se dérouler au niveau de leur mission » , a-t-il déclaré. Pour l’ONASSIM, cette immersion est désormais appelée à devenir une activité régulière et essentielle dans le renforcement des capacités de son personnel. Des acquis à transférer dans les services Du côté des participants, l’expérience a été marquée par des apprentissages pratiques, mais aussi par une remise en question personnelle. Halidou Zorome, agent à l’ONASSIM, dit avoir notamment retenu les enseignements relatifs à l’engagement patriotique, aux techniques d’intervention et au dépassement de soi. Les participants ont également reçu une instruction pratique sur le démontage et le remontage de la Kalachnikov et du pistolet automatique, ainsi qu’une formation au tir. Ajoutez Faso7 à vos sources sur Google. Cliquez ici : https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=faso7.com Pour le fonctionnaire, ces acquis ne doivent toutefois pas rester au CNEC. « Nous allons essayer de les transposer dans notre quotidien, c'est-à-dire dans nos différents services et dans nos différentes directions, pour que notre présence ici soit utilement transférée dans nos pratiques quotidiennes » , a-t-il expliqué. Cette volonté de dépasser les limites personnelles a également été évoquée par Mathieu Kaboré, agent à l’ONBAH. Il dit avoir découvert, au cours de l’immersion, des capacités qu’il ne pensait pas pouvoir mobiliser dans des conditions aussi exigeantes. « Tout est au niveau de la tête. Dès que tu programmes, tu dis que ça, tu ne peux pas faire, effectivement tu risques de ne pas pouvoir. Mais quand tu lâches au niveau de la tête, je crois que tout est possible » , a-t-il témoigné. Pour cet agent, les enseignements reçus pourraient être particulièrement utiles dans un office où certaines interventions peuvent être imprévisibles et nécessiter une forte disponibilité. Une formation liée aux missions stratégiques des deux offices-©Faso7 L’ONBAH a inscrit cette immersion dans sa volonté de renforcer les capacités opérationnelles de son personnel. Le commandant Wilfried Kabré, représentant le directeur général de l’office, a rappelé que l’institution intervient dans la réalisation d’infrastructures hydrauliques et d’aménagements hydro-agricoles, dans le cadre des objectifs de souveraineté alimentaire et hydrique. L’immersion devait ainsi contribuer à renforcer l’intégrité, la discipline et les valeurs patriotiques des agents afin qu’ils puissent mieux accomplir leurs missions, sur le terrain comme dans les bureaux. « On ne sort pas du CNEC comme on est entré au CNEC. On entre au CNEC avec des appréhensions et on sort au CNEC avec des valeurs » , a-t-il soutenu. Pour l’ONASSIM comme pour l’ONBAH, la réussite de cette immersion se mesurera surtout à la capacité des participants à transformer les valeurs apprises à Pô en comportements professionnels, en disponibilité et en engagement au service de leurs missions pour le Burkina Faso. items.title: Ondo electricity law will reduce poverty, boost agriculture — Arobo
items.description: By Dayo Johnson, Akure AKURE — The All Progressives Congress, APC, House of Representatives candidate for Owo/Ose Federal Constituency, Barr. Abdulghani Rotimi Arobo, has described the amended Ondo State Electricity Power Sector Law as a major step towards industrialisation, job creation and economic development. Arobo, in a statement issued by his campaign organisation, GRA4MHR, said the legislation, assented to by Governor Lucky Aiyedatiwa on August 13, 2026, would create opportunities for private investment, off-grid electricity solutions and sustainable power generation across the state. He commended Aiyedatiwa and the Ondo State House of Assembly for what he described as a proactive approach to reforming the state’s electricity sector. The APC candidate also credited the President Bola Tinubu administration with laying the foundation for the decentralisation of Nigeria’s electricity sector through the Electricity Act, which, he said, gave states greater responsibility for electricity generation and regulation. According to him, reliable electricity is critical to industrialisation and poverty reduction, particularly in rural and agrarian communities. Arobo said Ose Local Government Area, where some communities have reportedly been without electricity for more than a decade, should be prioritised under the new legal framework. He called on the state government to designate Ose as a pilot hub for alternative energy and off-grid solutions, including solar mini-grids and other renewable energy projects. He said such interventions would stimulate economic activities in agricultural communities by providing power for processing, storage and other value-added activities. Arobo also advocated the development of industrial and agricultural clusters across Owo and Ose, saying reliable electricity would help reduce post-harvest losses and support cottage industries. He further called for expanded technical training in renewable energy, arguing that the deployment of alternative energy systems could create jobs for young people in installation, maintenance and related services. The APC candidate stressed that the new electricity law should not remain a policy document but should be followed by aggressive implementation at the grassroots. He described the legislation as a product of federal and state collaboration and expressed optimism that effective implementation would help unlock Ondo State’s economic potential. Arobo pledged that his campaign would continue to make access to reliable electricity a major issue in the Owo/Ose constituency ahead of the general election. He further promised that, if elected and sworn into office, he would intensify efforts to attract interventions aimed at improving electricity supply and creating opportunities for industrial and agricultural development in the constituency. items.title: Guiriko : Fin de l’immersion patriotique pour 9 703 jeunes bacheliers
items.description: Guiriko : Fin de l’immersion patriotique pour 9 703 jeunes bacheliers Bobo-Dioulasso, 27 août 2026 (AIB) – Au total, 9 703 jeunes bacheliers ont achevé leur mois d’immersion patriotique obligatoire, lors d’une cérémonie présidée ce jeudi au stade omnisports Sangoulé-Lamizana de Bobo-Dioulasso par la gouverneure de la région du Guiriko, Mariama Konaté/ Gnanou. Durant 30 jours, les appelés, répartis sur 19 sites, dont 15 à Bobo-Dioulasso, deux à Orodara et deux à Houndé, ont été initiés aux valeurs de discipline, de solidarité, de respect et de vivre-ensemble. Cette immersion visait à renforcer leur sens du civisme, leur responsabilité et leur attachement à la patrie. Le camarade ministre délégué chargé des Ressources animales, Amadou Dicko, a pris part à la cérémonie de clôture. Au nom de ses camarades, l’appelée à l’immersion patriotique Fatimata Diallo a exprimé sa reconnaissance au Président du Faso, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, pour la place accordée à la jeunesse dans la construction du Burkina Faso. « Nous retenons de cette immersion, la discipline, l’intégrité et surtout l’amour de la patrie. Nous disons non à la fraude, à l’incivisme, oui au travail, oui à l’intégrité, oui à l’amour de la patrie. La formation s’achève mais notre engagement patriotique se poursuit et sera visible sur le terrain. Nous serons partout des Burkinabè dignes et intègres. Vive le Burkina Faso », a-t-elle déclaré. Dans son discours de clôture, la gouverneure Mariama Konaté/Gnanou a félicité les appelés pour leur participation à cette immersion, tout en les invitant à traduire les enseignements reçus en actes concrets. « Cette immersion n’était pas une punition. Notre pays traverse une période décisive de son histoire. Le Burkina Faso a besoin d’une jeunesse consciente et responsable qui place l’intérêt de la nation au-dessus de ses propres intérêts », a-t-elle déclaré. Selon elle, le patriotisme « ne se limite pas aux discours, mais se traduit par des actes au quotidien », notamment à travers la lutte contre la corruption, le travail bien fait et la volonté d’être utile à la nation. La gouverneure a également exhorté les jeunes à être des modèles dans leurs familles, leurs établissements et leurs futurs lieux de formation. « Soyez cette jeunesse qui rassemble plutôt que celle qui divise, celle qui construit plutôt que celle qui détruit. Retenez ceci : le Burkina Faso nouveau se bâtira grâce à votre dignité, votre engagement et votre patriotisme. Nos espoirs reposent sur vous. L’espoir du Président du Faso repose sur vous. Vous ne devez pas faillir », a-t-elle insisté. Elle a enfin salué l’ensemble des acteurs ayant contribué à la réussite de l’immersion patriotique obligatoire, ainsi que la patience et le soutien des parents des jeunes appelés. items.title: I bring 30 years of experience to make Dr Bawumia President – John Boadu on NPP National chair position
items.description: Former General Secretary of the New Patriotic Party (NPP), John Boadu, has pledged to deploy 30 years of political and organisational experience to help the party’s flagbearer, Dr Mahamudu Bawumia, win the 2028 presidential election. Mr Boadu made the pledge after filing his nomination to contest the NPP’s National Chairman position at the party’s national headquarters at Asylum Down in Accra on Thursday, August 27. Addressing supporters after submitting his nomination, Mr Boadu said his three decades of experience in party organisation, communication, strategy and discipline would provide the foundation for his bid to strengthen the NPP and return it to power. “I am bringing back 30 years’ worth of experience, 30 years of organisation, 30 years of communication, 30 years of strategising, 30 years of ensuring that there is discipline for us to win the 2028 election,” he said. He said his ambition was to build an effective party organisation capable of taking the campaign directly to the grassroots and delivering the parliamentary majority he believes will be crucial to the NPP’s return to government. Mr Boadu said the NPP under his leadership would concentrate heavily on its structures at constituency, electoral-area and polling-station levels. He argued that the party’s organisational machinery should take responsibility for grassroots mobilisation, allowing its presidential candidate to focus on the broader presidential campaign. “And for me, as for our flagbearer, we will let him sit somewhere. The only thing we will do is reaching constituency, electoral area, and polling station to win majority in Parliament,” he said. He linked the proposed grassroots strategy directly to Dr Bawumia’s presidential ambition, arguing that a strong parliamentary performance would help create the conditions for the NPP to win the presidency. “That will ensure that our flagbearer, His Excellency Dr Mahamudu Bawumia, is elected as President of Ghana,” Mr Boadu said.

items.description: BURKINA-NAHOURI-IMMERSION Nahouri/CNEC de Pô : 115 agents de l’ONASSIM et de l’ONBAH achèvent leur immersion patriotique Pô, 27 août 2026 (AIB)-Le Centre national d’entraînement commando (CNEC) de Pô a abrité, ce mercredi 26 août 2026, la cérémonie de clôture de l'immersion patriotique au profit de 115 agents de l’Office national de la sécurisation des sites miniers (ONASSIM) et de l’Office national des barrages et des aménagements hydro-agricoles (ONBAH). Initiée par les directions générales de l’Office national de la sécurisation des sites miniers (ONASSIM) et de l’Office national des barrages et des aménagements hydro-agricoles (ONBAH), cette formation de deux semaines visait à inculquer aux participants la discipline, l’intégrité, le sens du sacrifice, l'unité et la loyauté envers la Nation. Le représentant du directeur des cours, le capitaine Romaric Kagambéga, a salué le courage, la résilience et l'esprit d'équipe des stagiaires tout au long du séjour. « Ces hommes et ces femmes ont compris que le patriotisme se manifeste par le respect des règles, l'intégrité dans l'action, la solidarité et le service désintéressé », a-t-il souligné. Au nom de leurs camarades, Alidou Zorom (ONASSIM) et Mathieu Kaboré (ONBAH) ont exprimé leur gratitude envers les encadreurs et a affirmé que ces acquis renforceront leur efficacité professionnelle sur le terrain. Présidant conjointement la cérémonie, le directeur général de l'ONASSIM, le chef d'escadrons Arnauld W. Ouédraogo et le représentant du directeur général de l'ONBAH, le commandant W. P. Wilfried Kabré, ont rappelé les exigences liées aux missions de leurs institutions. « Servir dans une structure stratégique de l'État exige plus que des compétences techniques. Soyez des ambassadeurs du civisme. Combattez l'incivisme par votre exemplarité et placez l'intérêt du Burkina Faso au-dessus de toute considération personnelle », ont-ils exhorté. Le commandant du Centre national d’entraînement commando (CNEC) de Pô, le commandant Patrick Bado, a remercié les deux organismes pour la confiance accordée au centre. Il a invité les 115 agents de l'ONBAH et de l'ONASSIM à faire rayonner ces principes civiques acquise dans leurs services respectifs. Agence d’information du Burkina HKO/HB/OO

items.title: 7 countries that were banned from World Cup due to politics
items.description: The FIFA World Cup is often presented as a tournament that brings countries together through football. However, politics, war, international sanctions and government interference have repeatedly affected which nations are allowed to participate. Over the years, several countries have been prevented from taking part in the World Cup or its qualifying process because of political conflicts or actions involving their governments. Here are seven notable examples. 1. South Africa South Africa is one of the clearest examples of politics influencing World Cup participation. FIFA suspended the country in 1961 because of its apartheid system, which enforced racial segregation. The suspension was later reinstated, and South Africa was expelled from FIFA in 1976. The country’s exclusion lasted for several World Cup cycles until it was readmitted in 1992, following the dismantling of apartheid. South Africa eventually returned to the World Cup in 1998 and hosted the tournament in 2010. 2. Yugoslavia Yugoslavia was prevented from playing at the 1994 World Cup because of international sanctions imposed during the Yugoslav Wars. The United Nations imposed sanctions on Yugoslavia that included a prohibition on participation in international sporting events. As a result, the country was removed from the 1994 World Cup despite having a strong football tradition. The political break-up of Yugoslavia eventually resulted in several independent football nations, including Croatia, Slovenia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. 3. Russia Russia is the most prominent modern example of a country excluded from the World Cup because of an international political and military conflict. Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, FIFA and UEFA suspended Russian national teams and clubs from international competitions. The suspension prevented Russia from taking part in the 2022 World Cup play-offs and also kept the country out of the qualification process for the 2026 tournament. Russia remains suspended from FIFA and UEFA competitions. 4. Germany Germany was excluded from the 1950 World Cup in Brazil following the Second World War. The country had been defeated in the war just five years earlier, and its football association was not part of FIFA at the time of the tournament. Germany therefore missed the first World Cup held after the war, before returning to the competition in 1954. 5. Japan Japan was also excluded from the 1950 World Cup in the aftermath of the Second World War. Like Germany, Japan had been on the losing side of the conflict and was not permitted to participate in the tournament. Japan eventually returned to international football and made its World Cup debut in 1998. 6. Indonesia Indonesia was prevented from continuing in the 2018 World Cup qualifying campaign after FIFA suspended its football association over government interference. FIFA requires national football associations to operate independently from political authorities. Indonesia’s football association was suspended in 2015 after the Indonesian government intervened in its affairs. The suspension was eventually lifted in 2016 after the dispute was resolved, but Indonesia had already been removed from the 2018 qualifying process. 7. Kuwait Kuwait’s national team was also affected by political interference in football administration. FIFA suspended the Kuwait Football Association in 2015 after the country’s government introduced legislation that FIFA considered incompatible with its rules on the independence of national football associations. The suspension meant Kuwait could not complete its 2018 World Cup qualifying campaign. The ban was lifted in December 2017 after changes were made to Kuwait’s sports legislation. Vanguard News The post 7 countries that were banned from World Cup due to politics appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: A Republican Governor Tried to Heal American Politics. It Almost Broke Him.
items.description: O n August 9, 2023, Utah’s governor, Spencer Cox, found himself sitting across from Joe Biden in an armored presidential limousine as it idled in downtown Salt Lake City. Working up the nerve to pitch a far-fetched idea, he cleared his throat. “Mr. President, I know this might sound crazy,” Cox said, “but I think you should pardon Donald Trump.” Trump was, at the time, facing criminal charges in multiple jurisdictions. He was also the Republican frontrunner for president—a man who had promised to drive “Sleepy Joe” (a.k.a. “Enemy of the State,” a.k.a. “Most Corrupt President We’ve Ever Had,” a.k.a. “Worst President in the History of Our Country”) from the White House and imprison members of the “Biden crime family.” Cox had no loyalty to Trump; though a Republican, Cox had never voted for him and was hoping that his party would nominate someone else in 2024. But he believed that prosecuting a former president would deepen the country’s political crisis. A pardon by Biden, he argued, could deescalate tensions and interrupt the cycle of partisan retribution. To Cox’s surprise, Biden perked up at the suggestion. “You know, I’ve actually considered this for a while,” Biden said. “In fact, just this week as we were lying in bed, Jill and I had a long conversation about it.” Biden said that although people were “demanding justice” for Trump, he would seriously consider a pardon. Cox left the limousine convinced it was a real possibility. Of course, it never happened. A year later, after a gunman nearly killed Trump at a rally, Cox tried again from the other direction. In a letter to Trump, he wrote, “You have the opportunity to do something that no other person on earth can do right now: unify and save our country.” He offered his support for Trump’s candidacy, and encouraged him to respond to the moment with restraint and magnanimity. Trump happily accepted the endorsement, which Cox made public at a press conference several days later—but Trump the Great Unifier never materialized. Within days, he was back to railing against “crazy Nancy Pelosi” and riffing on illegal immigrants from insane asylums. [ Read: Trump has a warning for Spencer Cox ] Cox describes his experiences with the two presidents in his new book, Off Ramp: How to Be a Peacemaker in an Age of Contempt , which will be released next month. In the book, these episodes are framed as worthwhile—if ultimately unsuccessful—attempts at depolarization. “When I spoke with President Biden, I hoped he would choose mercy over escalation,” he writes. “When I wrote to President Trump, I hoped he would choose unity over retaliation. In both cases, things didn’t turn out quite the way I’d hoped.” “It would be fair to suggest I failed,” Cox ventures. Indeed it would. But he prefers not to think of it that way. Off Ramp is many things—a useful compendium of research on polarization and political violence, a candid memoir of Cox’s uneven attempts at peacemaking, a practical handbook for Americans who want to rediscover how to live with one another. But perhaps more than anything, it is an exercise in an almost-militant optimism that, to skeptics, might border on naivete. Cox told me that the book had been gestating for more than a decade. He spent years poring over political-science literature and testing his ideas in speeches and interviews; he even launched a project with the National Governors Association: “Disagree Better,” built around the book’s central arguments. But the book acquired a new urgency last year, when Charlie Kirk was assassinated in Utah and Cox was thrust into the international spotlight, where he called on Americans to step back from the brink. “At some point we have to find an off-ramp,” he said then, “or it’s going to get much, much worse.” When Kirk was murdered, Cox writes, “all of my research became painfully pertinent.” Throughout the book, and in a series of conversations I’ve had with him recently, Cox seems eager to dispel any notion that he has written another anodyne collection of bromides about bipartisanship and civility. The very word civility —with its connotation of, as he puts it, “a milquetoast politeness that would make Ned Flanders seem aggressive”—makes him cringe. What plagues America right now, in Cox’s telling, is not bad manners, or even political division, but contempt—the conviction that those who don’t share our opinions or values are beneath us and unworthy of good-faith engagement. “Healthy conflict is not a toxic symptom of democracy,” he writes. “It is foundational to it.” The proposition at the heart of Off Ramp is that political combat can be drained of contempt. As a civic aspiration, it’s hard to argue with. But at this moment? With these leaders? In a system that so strongly rewards reciprocal hatred? Cox knows as well as anyone how difficult it now is to practice the politics he’s preaching. L ast month I visited Cox on his family farm in central Utah, where he led me to the backyard. We sat with his wife, Abby, on wicker furniture overlooking a sprawling pasture with mountains in the distance. I wanted to ask Cox about a cryptic line in Off Ramp . It appears during the book’s account of the controversy that followed his 2024 endorsement of Trump. Allies and admirers publicly turned on him, he writes; people in his life privately urged him to reconsider. When Cox told one friend that he had prayed about the decision, the friend shot back, “Well, maybe you should pray again.” None of this surprised me. I had interviewed Cox in the governor’s mansion just a few days after he wrote that letter to Trump , and I remembered how conflicted he seemed even then—how he’d bounced from one rationalization to another, how he’d sounded like he was trying to justify the endorsement to himself as much as to me. I remembered the betrayal expressed by those who’d worked with him in the fight against polarization, as well as the edge in Cox’s voice when he said, “They’re very angry at me, and that’s fine.” The pile-on had clearly been unpleasant. But what caught my attention was a brief line in the book alluding to what the episode had been like for Cox. “These can be dark and lonely times,” he wrote. Dark and lonely? I asked Cox to elaborate, and he became quiet. “I knew there would be backlash,” he told me, tentatively. “It was much stronger than I expected.” He went on to describe a period of despair and depression that sounded, to my uncertified ear, almost clinical. Close friends and family members condemned his decision and distanced themselves from him. He feared his reputation as a champion of depolarization—developed over years of earnest, painstaking work—was ruined. He spent “a lot of long, dark nights,” he told me, wishing things could go back to how they were. Cox’s faith, usually a source of comfort in such moments, seemed to make the experience even more fraught. He believes God answers prayers, and he said he’d prayed intensely over whether to endorse. He was quick to clarify that he was not claiming that God wanted Trump to win—but he felt strongly that he was supposed to offer his support to the candidate, for reasons he couldn’t entirely articulate. As the governor spoke, I noticed that Abby, who had been largely silent throughout our conversation, was pursing her lips. I asked her what she remembered about that summer, and she started to cry. “In our marriage, I have never seen him like that,” she told me. She was especially hurt that some of the people who criticized Cox most harshly, dismissing him as craven and disingenuous, were those who had the closest relationships with him. “The people who know you best should trust that you aren’t just doing this on a whim.” I noted that, back in 2024, Abby herself had not been a fan of her husband’s endorsement. “I’m still not,” she said. “We see things differently. But I trusted him.” Cox now believes that he was guided to improve his relationship with Trump in 2024 so that he would be prepared to deal with the defining crisis of his governorship a year later: Kirk’s assassination. [ Read: A disorienting weekend with the women of Turning Point ] During and after the tense 33-hour manhunt for Kirk’s killer, Cox was able to coordinate closely with the Trump administration while also using his high-profile news conferences to offer necessary counterprogramming to the This-means-war rhetoric coming from much of MAGA world. Cox urged calm, condemned all political violence, and called for his fellow Americans to reject politics that “feels like rage.” This balancing act was widely praised. As my colleague David Graham wrote at the time, “In any other state,” local politicians might have either become targets for Trump “or leapt to inflame the situation. But the Beehive State’s governor is perhaps the most consistent voice of calm and conciliation in the GOP.” More important, Cox notes, his performance won approval from the president, who largely let the governor lead the official response without interference. Cox’s critics will no doubt find this narrative self-serving, perhaps even grandiose. But Cox doesn’t seem to care how it looks. “Charlie’s death could easily have been the match that lit the tinderbox of a nation,” he writes in his book. “However, that didn’t happen, and I hope that at least one small reason for that was the positive relationship that has developed between the president and me. It might have made it easier for him to trust my leadership and allow an off ramp to de-escalation.” W hen it came time for Cox to give me a tour of his hometown, he walked me to an old, beat-up pickup truck parked out front and told me to get in. The choice of vehicle was clearly a stunt for my benefit—Cox writes about learning to drive a 1974 Chevy on the farm when he was only 5—but the contrivance didn’t bother me until he casually admitted that this was only the third time he had driven a car since becoming governor five years ago. I buckled my seat belt. It was the day before Pioneer Day, when Utahns celebrate Brigham Young’s arrival in Salt Lake Valley, and people were already saving their spots on Main Street for the town’s regionally famous parade. Fairview was settled by Cox’s great-great-great-great grandfather in 1859, and his family is practically built into the infrastructure of the place. He showed me the cemetery where he installed a flagpole for an Eagle Scout project, and the phone company that had been run by the Coxes since 1919, and the various houses he had grown up in. At my request, we stopped at the Fairview Museum of History and Art, where kitschy pioneer artifacts were arranged in displays with delightfully literal names: the “Tool Room” contained an array of old tools; the “Dentist Room” featured (you guessed it) old dental equipment. An older woman working at the front desk beamed at Cox and remarked how nice it was to see him “all grown-up.” Cox has deployed Fairview as a device in his speeches for years, and it plays a central role in Off Ramp . He uses his hometown as a stand-in for the qualities America urgently needs: thick community, strong institutions, and the prioritizing of our obligations to one another above the wanton inflammations of politics. This is hardly an original trope in politicians’ memoirs, but Cox seems to come by his boosterism honestly. He writes that his parents’ divorce, when he was 10, sent him into a spiral of anger, fear, and profound sadness. “Many times,” he writes, “I thought that the world would be a better place without me.” What carried him through was Fairview: the next-door neighbors whose refrigerator was always open to him, the uncle who took him into the mountains and showed him how to herd sheep, the teacher who taught him to love books, the scoutmaster who took him camping. When he felt on the verge of giving up, he writes, they “made my situation their business.” When Cox became lieutenant governor in 2013, he insisted on keeping his family in Fairview and regularly commuted the roughly 200 miles to Salt Lake City and back—three hours round trip—rather than surrendering his life there. Off Ramp is dedicated “to my family, my friends, and my Fairview.” Lately, though, Cox has worried that his sanctuary has been breached. The town Facebook group, once a clearinghouse for reports of loose chickens and missing Amazon packages, is periodically littered with comments about Trump and immigration. In the book, Cox describes watching right-wing talk radio transform his father-in-law, a local rancher, from a “beautiful, gracious man” into an angry, combative crank perpetually spoiling for a political fight. (Eventually, a family intervention would pull the man away from talk radio and back to his old self.) Cox himself can relate to the deleterious effects of excessive political-news consumption: In one admirably unflattering passage, he writes about his own addiction to Twitter and its “information heroin.” It got so bad that he had to delete social-media apps from his phone. Cox seems to recognize the dangers of publishing a book like this. No matter how many self-effacing caveats he includes, he risks looking like he’s holding himself up as a role model of civic virtue. The truth, he says, is that the precepts he articulates don’t come naturally to him. “I’m a hothead,” he told me. “I’ve gotten punched in the face. I’ve punched people in the face.” Once he was even kicked out of a game while coaching his kid’s flag-football game. “That’s who I am.” He said he works to temper those impulses, which seem omnipresent in our politics, but that he doesn’t always succeed. “It’s hard to be the Disagree Better guy, because you’re under a microscope,” Cox said. “When I say something disrespectful or lash out, people pounce.” In Off Ramp , he revisits a moment at a Utah Republican convention, when, after being booed by Trump supporters, he snapped: “Maybe you hate that I don’t hate enough.” The retort was so satisfying in the moment. “The words coming out of my mouth felt good,” he writes. But he later came to regret it—he had answered contempt with contempt, making it that much harder for him and his opponents to understand one another. In the weeks afterward, he personally apologized to some of the people who had booed him. A similar episode took place at a Disagree Better event at George Washington University, when a student confronted him over Utah’s ban on gender-affirming care for minors, linking it to suicide rates among transgender kids. Cox responded defensively, accusing the student of “bad faith.” “I want these kids to thrive,” he said. “I want these kids to be successful.” But, he continued, “I think there’s a better way to do that than having genital-mutilation surgeries before they’re 18." Cox, quickly catching himself, said he should have given his interlocutor the last word, and invited the student backstage after the event to keep talking. But even as Cox tries to model healthy political debate, he rejects the idea—often floated by his critics—that “disagreeing better” means never staking out controversial positions or supporting divisive policies. “I’m going to be a partisan,” he told me. “I want my team to win. When my team wins, we’re going to try to implement those things.” Politics, he told me, doesn’t have to rid itself of partisanship to become less contemptuous. When I asked Cox whether he ever worries that his optimism is misplaced, he answered immediately: “I think about that every day.” He does not pretend, he told me, that “a book from a governor of Utah is going to change the course of history.” But he remains stubbornly hopeful that America’s political culture is ready for a reset. He cites letters from people who have reconciled with their parents after politics had poisoned their relationships, and Disagree Better workshops attended by hundreds of legislators and policy makers. He’s convinced that the movement is growing, though he concedes that the evidence is mostly anecdotal. “We’ll have an actual measuring stick soon,” he told me, “when we see if people buy the book.”

items.title: Mines-Guinée: Predictive Discovery devient officiellement PDI Gold Limited et affiche de grandes ambitions
items.description: Le paysage minier guinéen enregistre un nouveau tournant. La société minière Predictive Discovery Limited (anciennement Sycamore) a officiellement changé de raison sociale pour devenir PDI Gold Limited. C’est entre autres, ce qu’il faut retenir à l'issue d'une assemblée générale extraordinaire des actionnaires qui s'est tenue le 21 août dernier, suivie d’un enregistrement auprès du régulateur australien. Selon les informations publiées ensuite sur les plateformes de la société, ce changement de nom, validé par les actionnaires, sera effectif dès le 9 septembre 2026 sur les places boursières de Sydney (ASX) et de Toronto (TSX). Le groupe a toutefois précisé que son code boursier demeure inchangé sous le libellé « PDI », tout comme son nouveau portail numérique officiel (www.pdigold.com). Et que parallèlement, un regroupement d'actions à raison d'une pour cinq a également été adopté par les investisseurs afin d'ajuster la structure financière de l'entreprise. De la mine de Kiniéro au méga-projet Bankan, une dynamique de croissance accélérée Cette mue institutionnelle intervient dans un contexte opérationnel particulièrement dynamique pour le groupe en Guinée. PDI Gold consolide sa position de producteur aurifère émergent de premier plan en Afrique de l'Ouest grâce au succès de ses actifs phares dans le pays. Entrée en production fin 2025, avec une première coulée d'or enregistrée en décembre et le lancement de la production commerciale en février 2026, la mine d'or de Kiniéro constitue aujourd'hui le principal moteur opérationnel de l'entreprise. Exploité par extraction conventionnelle à ciel ouvert (notamment sur le gisement de Sabali Sud), le site dispose d'une usine de cyanuration en pulpe (CIL) moderne d'une capacité de 5 millions de tonnes par an (Mtpa). Il devrait ainsi produire en moyenne 139 000 onces d'or par an sur une durée de vie initiale estimée à neuf ans, tout en générant des flux de trésorerie à court terme essentiels pour le financement du groupe. Au-delà de Kiniéro, la stratégie de PDI Gold repose sur le développement du titanesque projet Bankan, considéré comme l'un des plus importants gisements aurifères non encore développés sur le continent africain. Et à terme, le groupe ambitionne de franchir le cap des 400 000 onces produites par an à l'horizon 2029 depuis son pôle guinéen, Bankan tablant pour sa part sur environ 250 000 onces annuelles sur une période de plus de douze ans. Visite gouvernementale et consécration du contenu local Cette montée en puissance industrielle s'accompagne d'un renforcement des liens de partenariat avec les autorités guinéennes. La semaine dernière, la mine de Kiniéro a eu l'honneur d'accueillir une importante délégation gouvernementale conduite par le Ministre des Mines et de la Géologie, Bona Sylla et son collègue Moussa Moïse Sylla, Ministre de la Culture, du Tourisme et de l'Artisanat. Cette visite de terrain a permis de présenter aux membres du gouvernement les performances opérationnelles du site ainsi que ses retombées socio-économiques matérialisées par la création d’emplois locaux et le dynamisme du développement communautaire. Selon le compterendu de cette visite, saluant les avancées réalisées par les équipes de PDI Gold Guinée, M. Bouna Sylla, a tenu à souligner l'exemplarité de la démarche. « Je félicite la direction et les employés de Sycamore (désormais PDI Gold Guinée ndlr) pour les progrès accomplis. Je salue également leur engagement en faveur du contenu local, de la formation des jeunes et du développement des petites entreprises et des communautés. Il est de notre responsabilité de faire de nos ressources naturelles un véritable moteur de transformation et de progrès économique pour la Guinée», déclare-t-il. Avec cette nouvelle identité boursière et des bases industrielles davantage ancrées dans le basin aurifère de Siguiri, PDI Gold Limited se positionne plus que jamais comme un acteur incontournable de l'économie minière guinéenne.
