items.title: Télimélé : Attaque à main armée, des passagers d’un véhicule en provenance du Sénégal dépouillés à Kaaba
items.description: Une attaque à main armée a été perpétrée dans la nuit du mercredi 26 au jeudi 27 août 2026 dans la préfecture de Télimélé. Six individus armés, vêtus de tenues militaires, selon nos informations, ont pris pour cible un véhicule de transport en provenance du Sénégal, dans la localité de Kaaba, relevant de la sous-préfecture de Gougoudjé. Plusieurs passagers ont été violentés et dépouillés de fortes sommes d’argent, de téléphones et d’autres objets de valeur. Selon les témoignages recueillis, les assaillants ont tendu une embuscade au véhicule avant de tirer sur ses pneus afin de l’immobiliser. Parmi les victimes figure Mohamed Camara, qui revenait du Sénégal et devait rejoindre Sangaréah, dans la préfecture de Pita. Revenant sur le déroulement de l’attaque, il explique que plusieurs signes inhabituels avaient précédé l’embuscade « Lorsque nous sommes arrivés vers Kaaba, nous avons rencontré une voiture de marque Verso qui roulait à vive allure. Son chauffeur nous a demandé de nous arrêter, comme s’il voulait nous alerter, mais nous n’avons pas compris son message et il a continué son chemin. Ensuite, un deuxième véhicule nous a dépassés à vive allure, en provenance de Conakry. Un peu plus tard, nous avons aperçu deux motos qui venaient dans notre direction. Leurs occupants nous ont dit que notre bagage était tombé. Mais notre chauffeur n’en a pas tenu compte, parce qu’il savait que les bagages étaient bien attachés. » a-t-il expliqué. « C’est alors que les assaillants seraient passés à l’action. Un premier tir aurait visé le pneu avant du véhicule sans l’atteindre. Le second coup de feu, en revanche, aurait atteint le pneu arrière, contraignant le chauffeur à s’arrêter, directement, nous avons été immobilisés. Les assaillants ont alors fait sortir le chauffeur et tous les autres passagers. Ils nous ont ordonné de nous coucher à terre », poursuit Mohamed Camara. Les victimes ont ensuite été systématiquement dépouillées. Mohamed Camara affirme avoir réussi à dissimuler son iPhone, mais son sac contenant 400 000 francs CFA et 500 000 francs guinéens, ainsi que deux autres téléphones, a été emporté. Une autre passagère aurait perdu un million de francs CFA, après avoir été brutalisée par les assaillants. Ces derniers auraient également fouillé l’ensemble du véhicule et emporté plusieurs autres sommes d’argent ainsi que divers objets de valeur. La violence de l’attaque a particulièrement marqué les passagers « Ils nous ont administré des coups, tout en proférant des injures et des menaces de mort. Ils ont dit que quiconque lèverait la tête serait abattu. Un Oustaz qui était parmi nous a été violemment tabassé et son visage est enflé. L’un des assaillants disait que s’il refusait d’obéir, ils allaient tirer sur lui. À ce moment-là, nous n’avions plus aucun espoir de vivre. Mais dès qu’ils ont terminé leur opération, ils sont partis », témoigne Mohamed Camara. Cette nouvelle attaque survient environ 24 heures après un autre braquage enregistré sur la route nationale Télimélé-Kindia. Dans la nuit du lundi au mardi, aux environs de 22 heures, des hommes armés circulant à moto avaient pris pour cible un véhicule de transport en commun qui quittait le marché hebdomadaire de Kambanya, dans la préfecture de Télimélé, à destination de Kindia. Les victimes de cette première attaque ont saisi la Brigade de recherches de la gendarmerie de Kindia, qui avait annoncé l’ouverture d’une enquête.

items.title: NRSA calls for urgent action on road infrastructure deficiencies
items.description: Director of Regulations, Inspections and Compliance at the National Road Safety Authority (NRSA), Kwame Kodua Attuahene, has called for urgent action to address infrastructure deficiencies within Ghana’s road network as part of efforts to improve road safety and reduce road fatalities. Mr Atuahene acknowledged that Ghana has made visible improvements in its road infrastructure but stressed that the country’s road network remains far from perfect. Speaking on the Joy FM Super Morning Show on Thursday, August 27, as part of Joy Sustainability Month, he said deficiencies in road infrastructure continue to be an important part of the road safety challenge and require sustained attention from government and relevant institutions. “We do not have a perfect road network. Even though we’ve seen some visible improvements, we are not at a stage where we cannot go to school,” he said. According to him, concerns about road infrastructure have been raised repeatedly over the past three to four years, with calls for government to take the necessary steps to address identified gaps. The comments formed part of a broader discussion on Ghana’s road safety performance and the factors contributing to road crashes. Mr Atuahene noted that road safety should not be assessed solely by looking at the absolute number of fatalities. He explained that there are three major indicators used to assess road safety performance: the absolute number of deaths, the fatality rate based on the number of vehicles, and population risk. While the absolute number of road deaths may show an increase, he said the other indicators provide a different picture of the country’s performance. “Fatality rates, which is death by 10,000 vehicles, there’s been an improvement from about 9.3 deaths per 10,000 vehicles to about 6,” he said. He added that population risk had also recorded an improvement. Mr Atuahene said vehicle and population numbers change over time, making it important to analyse fatalities in relation to the number of vehicles and the size of the population. He noted that the data showed a generally declining trend in the relevant indicators between 2016 and 2023, although the trend changed in 2024. Despite the improvement in fatality rates, he cautioned that the country should not become complacent. “Every death that occurs on our roads is one that keeps all of us to worry about,” he said. He called for renewed urgency among institutions and stakeholders responsible for road safety, stressing that the existence of a national strategy should translate into stronger action. Mr Atuahene also rejected the idea that responsibility for road safety should rest entirely with one institution. He explained that road safety involves several interconnected areas, including infrastructure, enforcement, vehicle conditions and road-user behaviour. He said deficiencies on the infrastructure side must be addressed alongside other factors contributing to crashes. “If there are deficiencies from the infrastructure side as the report seeks to suggest, you may be able to answer those,” he said.

items.title: DHQ debunks AI-generated video targeting Chief of Defence Staff
items.description: By Kingsley Omonobi The Defence Headquarters (DHQ) has debunked a fabricated video generated with artificial intelligence and falsely portraying the Chief of Defence Staff (CDS), General Olufemi Oluyede, as making statements suggesting partisan political support. In a press statement, the Director of Defence Information, Major General Samaila Uba, said the video was fake and did not emanate from the Chief of Defence Staff. The DHQ stated unequivocally that the statements attributed to the CDS in the video were false and should be completely disregarded. According to the statement, the video was a product of AI-generated manipulation allegedly designed to deceive and mislead members of the public, misrepresent the position of the Chief of Defence Staff and bring the Armed Forces of Nigeria into disrepute. “For the avoidance of doubt, the Armed Forces of Nigeria remains a professional, apolitical and non-partisan institution, committed to the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria and the defence of the nation,” the statement said. The Defence Headquarters strongly condemned what it described as the deliberate creation and circulation of the fake video, warning those responsible, as well as individuals knowingly amplifying the material, to desist forthwith. Members of the public were urged to disregard the video and rely only on information released through official Defence Headquarters communication channels. The DHQ listed its verified channels as its Facebook page, Defence Headquarters Nigeria; X handle, DHQNigeria; Instagram account, DefenceHQ; WhatsApp channel, Defence Headquarters Nigeria; and YouTube channel, DefenceTV-Nigeria. items.title: Nepal flood death toll climbs to 359 as around 1,000 remain missing
items.description: Devastating floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have killed at least 359 people, Nepali police said in an update on Thursday, a day after the disaster. “As of 5pm [on] Thursday, 359 people have died,” Nepal Police said in a statement. Chinese state media had earlier reported “major casualties” from a mudslide at a Tibet border hub with three dead, taking the total killed to at least 362. A terrifying clip of surveillance video from the Chinese side of the frontier shows a massive wall of mud and debris crashing over a building several stories high on Wednesday morning, engulfing it as dozens of people ran for their lives below. The surge swept away buses and cars like they were toys. Many of the missing are foreign tourists, officials said of the disaster, which the US Geological Survey believes was caused by a glacial collapse that sent a flow of debris engulfing areas along the way. The tsunami-like rumble of water and mud struck villages and towns on the path of two rivers — Bhote Koshi and Trishuli. When Nepal’s death toll stood at 273, 823 people, including 579 Nepali and foreign tourists, remained out of contact, according to the country’s disaster agency. These included nearly 100 Chinese nationals, according to Beijing’s foreign ministry. The Chinese embassy was “seeking further verification” from Nepali authorities, ministry spokesman Lin Jian told reporters. Later, about 100 missing Indian visitors and 25 Chinese workers were located by rescuers in Nepal, authorities said. Across the border, Chinese state media said 558 people, including 260 foreigners, were still missing. Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah left by road for Bidur in one of the worst-affected districts of Nuwakot to assess the flood situation, his office said on social media. Raju Bhadel, 56, a businessman in Nuwakot, recounted receiving a call from his brother-in-law in distress. “They were crying and said their entire house had been swept away. Three family members were rescued, but his brother is still missing,” he said. Also at Nuwakot, teacher Manok Mishra witnessed “nine trucks being swept away by the floods, including people”. This frame grab taken from video released by the Armed Police Force of Nepal on August 26, 2026 shows rescue workers carrying a person after massive floods and landslides in Rasuwa. —AFP ‘Inland tsunami’ Rescuers waded through mud and sludge to look for survivors after floodwaters buried the lower floors of multi-storey buildings. Among those hunting for their missing family members was Subash Khatani, who told AFP he was looking for his big brother. “He is among the missing from Rasuwa. That’s why we are out to search for him,” he said. Among the missing tourists from more than two dozen countries, 177 were from India, 63 were from the United States, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada. Others included tourists from Malaysia, the Netherlands, Portugal, South Africa and South Korea, Nepal’s tourism board said. Hiking company Himalayan Glacier told AFP that 47 people from a group, including two children, were missing in Nepal. “Our teams are checking hospitals where victims are coming in,” said the company’s director Sanket Pandey. The sudden rush of mud and debris was “like an inland tsunami, travelling nearly 170 kilometres down the Bhote Koshi valley into Central Nepal”, said environmental historian Ruth Gamble of La Trobe University. “It is a popular route for international tourists travelling from Kathmandu to Lhasa,” she added. “It was a huge gush of mud coming straight towards us,” said Keshav Prasad Baral, a 68-year-old survivor being treated in a Nepali hospital. “As it got closer, it kept rising higher and higher. When I saw it enter our home, I tried to grab my wife’s hand and take her to the terrace. But she was swept away by the mud.” A helicopter ferried him to safety four hours later. “My wife is still somewhere beneath the mud,” he added. “She’s gone.” Another survivor said he saved himself by clinging to a mango tree as he watched the house where he had been working disappear. Rasuwa, in the north of Nepal, was the first district to be affected. But deaths have been reported from seven Nepali districts in total as the floodwaters raged through to Chitwan in the south, on the border with India. “There is devastation everywhere we look,” said Tula Bahadur BK, a health worker in Rasuwa. “The settlements next to the river have been completely swept away. Five of my own relatives are missing.” The Nepali Army was carrying out flights and had rescued scores of people, while others living near the river in danger zones had been told to relocate. China’s leader Xi Jinping said that “the most urgent task is doing everything possible to search for and rescue the missing people”, according to CCTV . Tibet government officials mobilised nearly 800 emergency workers and 150 vehicles as well as sniffer dogs and speed boats to help the rescue efforts, China’s state-run news agency Xinhua said. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) said it was dispatching emergency supplies including blankets, first aid kits, stretchers and body bags. “Entire villages and market areas have been wiped out,” said David Fisher, the Nepal head of IFRC. The US State Department said it was sending a disaster response adviser and providing assistance of $500,000. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said details on the disaster were scant. “Nepal … is a developing country,” he said. “It doesn’t have the resources that an event like that would have in Australia, so information is difficult.” UN teams and partners were sending supplies and personnel to support affected Nepali communities, Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said. Glacial collapse The cause of the disaster was not immediately clear in the hours after it occurred early on Wednesday, but the US Geological Survey said it was a glacial collapse that caused seismic activity and the “catastrophic” downstream impacts in Nepal and Tibet. “This event was initially reported as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake,” it said. “Additional analysis of nearby seismic stations, long-period seismic waves, and satellite imagery led to the determination that the seismic event was instead a glacial collapse and debris flow, and that no earthquake had occurred.” Climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risks of glacial lake floods and glacial collapses. Residents look at a street submerged by mud following flash floods and a landslide disaster in Devighat, in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on August 26, 2026. —AFP Qianggong Zhang, head of climate and environmental risks at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), warned of the potential for a second flood. “With a blockage still lodged upstream on the Nepal-China border river, authorities warn a second flood may occur,” he told AFP. Many trekking companies were not running tours during the monsoon season, but there remain significant numbers of travellers, including pilgrims, in the region. Experts cautioned that a lingering blockage in a river could produce an additional flood. Among sites hit by the flood was Syabrubesi, the gateway to the popular trekking areas, as well as by pilgrims travelling to the base of Mount Kailash, a holy site for Buddhists and Hindus. Traffic authorities in Tibet’s Shigatse said roads in the area were “at risk of mudslides and unsafe for passage”. Buddhist spiritual leader the Dalai Lama said that he was praying for all those killed in devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet. “I pray for all those who have lost their lives, and offer my sympathy and heartfelt condolences to the bereaved and to all those affected by this tragedy,” he said in a statement.

items.title: Coopération bilatérale: le Vice-Premier ministre, ministre en charge des Affaires étrangères du Royaume de Belgique en visite au Burkina Faso pour consolider une coopération basée sur la sincérité
items.description: Le Vice-Premier ministre, ministre des Affaires étrangères, des Affaires européennes et de la Coopération au Développement du Royaume de Belgique, SEM Maxime PRÉVOT est arrivé dans l'après-midi du 26 août 2026 à Ouagadougou. Accueilli par le ministre des Affaires étrangères le Camarade Karamoko Jean Marie TRAORE, l'autorité belge est au pays des Hommes intègres pour une visite d’amitié et de travail de 72 heures. L'accueil à l'aéroport international de Ouagadougou a été suivi d'une audience entre les deux hommes, en compagnie de leurs proches collaborateurs au ministère des Affaires étrangères. Les échanges ont permis de mettre en exergue le dynamisme et la qualité de la coopération bilatérale entre le Burkina Faso et le Royaume de Belgique, une coopération établie depuis plus de 50 ans et qui s’opère principalement à travers l’Agence belge de développement (Enabel). Selon le Vice-Premier ministre, ministre des Affaires étrangères, des Affaires européennes et de la Coopération au Développement du Royaume de Belgique, sa visite s'inscrit dans une démarche de renforcement de la coopération entre son pays et le Burkina Faso, dans un esprit de maturité, d'humilité et de sincérité. >, a souligné SEM Maxime PRÉVOT à l'entame des échanges. Cette approche de l'autorité belge a été saluée à juste titre par le ministre des Affaires étrangères burkinabè, qui a saisi l'occasion pour faire un exposé clair et détaillé sur le contexte de l'installation de la crise sécuritaire au Burkina Faso et l'engagement des autorités actuelles pour y faire face, grâce à une dynamique endogène et à la collaboration avec des partenaires sincères. >, a indiqué le Camarade ministre des Affaires étrangères à son hôte. D'autres sujets en lien avec la dynamique de la Confédération AES et les perspectives de la coopération entre le Burkina Faso et l'Union Européenne dont la capitale belge abrite le siège, ont également meublé les échanges entre SEM Maxime PRÉVOT et le Chef de la diplomatie burkinabè. Au terme des échanges, le Vice-Premier ministre, ministre des Affaires étrangères, des Affaires européennes et de la Coopération au Développement du Royaume de Belgique, dit être édifié et a indiqué que son pays reste engagé à investir « au Burkina Faso, avec le Burkina Faso, mais pas à la place du Burkina Faso ». C'est ainsi la preuve que les relations diplomatiques entre les deux pays demeurent marquées par le respect de la souveraineté, des positions et des choix stratégiques de chaque partie, ainsi que par la sincérité et la transparence dans le dialogue. La coopération entre le Burkina Faso et le Royaume de Belgique s'étend sur de nombreux secteurs prioritaires tels que le développement économique, l'agriculture, l'environnement, la santé, l'éducation, l'entreprenariat, ainsi que la coopération décentralisée, culturelle et inter-universitaire. La réorganisation en cours de la couverture diplomatique belge dans le monde, marquée par la fermeture de plusieurs missions, n’a pas affecté l’Ambassade de Belgique à Ouagadougou. Les autorités belges envisagent au contraire d’en faire un hub consulaire dans la sous-région. La visite d'amitié et de travail du Vice-Premier ministre, ministre des Affaires étrangères, des Affaires européennes et de la Coopération au Développement du Royaume de Belgique au Burkina Faso, sera également marquée par d'autres audiences avec des autorités burkinabè et des sorties terrain. DCRP/MAE

items.title: The Painter Who Shaped Rothko
items.description: T he evolution of European modern art can be explained as a story of susceptible young people falling under others’ spells and then asking, What can I do with this? How can I convert it to my purposes? What’s remarkable is how often the main chapters of this story have unfolded in coastal or mountain retreats. Think of Claude Monet on the Normandy coast, wrestling with the influence of his mentor Eugène Boudin. Or Henri Matisse staying in Saint-Tropez with his mentor Paul Signac, before breaking with Signac’s neo-impressionist style and co-inventing fauvism. Or Pablo Picasso, goaded into radicalism by the latest bizarre creations of Matisse, retreating to the Spanish mountain village of Gósol and, mere months later, beginning work on his proto-cubist masterpiece, Les Demoiselles d’Avignon . All of these key episodes happened in agreeable resorts, seaside ports, and villages, far from the sophisticated cities assumed to have been the cauldrons of modernism. Modern art in America is no different. Its story can scarcely be told without reference to artists summering on the Atlantic Coast, including Winslow Homer, Marsden Hartley, and Edward Hopper in Maine and Massachusetts and Jackson Pollock, Lee Krasner , and Willem de Kooning on Long Island. Beginning in the early 1930s, three Americans—Milton Avery, Mark Rothko, and Adolph Gottlieb—began spending summers together on Cape Ann, along the coast of northeast Massachusetts. They loved the gritty authenticity of Gloucester, the nation’s oldest fishing port. Cape Ann’s distinctive, undulant geography combined pungent industry and village intensity with Atlantic immensity of sea and sky. The story of the relationships among these artists, in particular between the older Avery and the now–stratospherically famous Rothko, shows us American modernism in its moment of greatest transition. Avery was the mentor figure, the one destined, in the usual telling of this story, to be eclipsed. Whereas Rothko is a regular subject of museum retrospectives in Europe and North America, and his paintings can sell at auction for as much as $98 million, Avery remains relatively unknown outside of the U.S. (The most expensive Avery sold at auction was a little more than $6 million, in 2022.) But are we telling the right story about Avery if we cast him in this role? Milton Avery, Gorton’s Dock , 1931–34. Gouache on brown paper. Private collection. Jeremy Lawson Photography. © 2026 The Milton Avery Trust / Artists Rights Society, New York. Left: Mark Rothko, Untitled (wharf, Gloucester, Massachusetts) , 1934. Watercolor on construction paper. Collection of Christopher Rothko, 1076.25-27. © 1998 Kate Rothko Prizel & Christopher Rothko / Artists Rights Society, New York. Right: Adolph Gottlieb, Gloucester Street , c. 1934. Oil on linen mounted on board. Adolph and Esther Gottlieb Foundation. © 2026 Adolph and Esther Gottlieb Foundation / Licensed by VAGA at Artists Rights Society, New York. Certainly, when Rothko and Gottlieb, during World War II, turned to abstraction, they broke from Avery and, in short order, became central figures in a mid-century revolution—one that transformed modern art from a marginal activity to a cultural phenomenon attracting cash, prestige, and international acclaim. Avery wasn’t exactly forgotten in all of this, but he has long been overlooked. He had first come to Gloucester in 1920, returning regularly during the summer until 1945. It’s where he met his wife, a fellow artist named Sally Michel. The fishing port was known as a bustling artists’ colony. In the 19th century, Homer and Fitz Henry Lane had spent productive time there, as had Hopper, Cecilia Beaux, and Stuart Davis in the 20th. So Avery was far from alone as he strolled around the harbor with his sketchbook and retired at night to rudimentary rooms lacking toilets and bathtubs. In 1932, he and Sally, who was pregnant with their only child, were joined on Cape Ann by Rothko—at the time called Markus Rothkowitz; he began using the name Mark Rothko in 1940—and Gottlieb. Avery was in his element in Gloucester. Confident, good-humored, and in the noontime of life, he sat comfortably on his own shadow. Unlike his protégés, he was not especially intellectual. He was a taciturn pragmatist with a gentle sense of humor. He had a dog called Picasso. To those who said modern art was ugly and hard to appreciate, he would answer: “Olives taste ugly, too, until you learn to enjoy them.” [ Read: Did Marcel Duchamp ruin art? ] The two younger men felt his support, but he didn’t force his ideas on them. According to Eliza Rathbone, the curator of an exhibit about the trio’s seaside summers currently on view at the Cape Ann Museum, Avery “never uttered a word of advice or instruction to any painter other than ‘do another one.’” He set an example: how to be a modern artist, yes. But also: how to be a husband and father, how to carry on. His very reticence was liberating. The three men had become friends in New York, where they would gather in the evenings to sketch and discuss art at the Averys’ Lincoln Square apartment. “I cannot tell you what it meant for us during those early years to be made welcome in those memorable studios,” Rothko would later recall. Adolph Gottlieb, Untitled (Mark Rothko with Mandolin) , c. 1932. Crayon on paper. Adolph and Esther Gottlieb Foundation. © 2026 Adolph and Esther Gottlieb Foundation / Licensed by VAGA at Artists Rights Society, New York. In Gloucester, they explored the port, with its wharves and warehouses and fish-processing facilities, filling sketchbooks and painting small-scale works in watercolor. A total solar eclipse that August provided fodder for Avery, who made an amusing watercolor showing people on Good Harbor Beach looking at the celestial phenomenon through smoked glasses and colored film. Milton Avery, Eclipse Watchers , c. 1932. Watercolor on paper. Private collection. Jeremy Lawson Photography. © 2026 The Milton Avery Trust / Artists Rights Society, New York. That first summer together was bookended by major life events back in New York. The Depression had flooded the streets with the unemployed. Gottlieb married in June. In October, as memories of summer receded, Sally gave birth to a daughter, and a few weeks later, Rothko married. In those days, Rothko and Gottlieb would study Avery’s paintings and, according to Sally Avery, “take them apart.” On Cape Ann, they watched him treat the beach as a backdrop against which he placed monumental, thick-hipped figures, arranging areas of pattern (umbrellas, beachwear) against flat, colored shapes in compositions with shifting horizon lines. Following Avery’s example, they experimented with gouache and watercolor applied to colored construction paper. The Averys and Gottliebs returned in the summer of 1933, and were joined by the Rothkos in 1934. The Depression was biting hard, but the artists’ life in Gloucester remained simple and uncorrupted. “We saw each other day in and day out,” Sally recalled of those years. “Evenings we’d gather to have a cup of tea and look at our day’s work. There was no talk of selling—only of painting.” “I always thought Avery was a great artist,” Gottlieb would later say. “I always regarded him as a brilliant colorist and draftsman, a solitary figure working against the stream.” Gottlieb was right. Avery was one of the 20th century’s most original colorists. His expansive compositions were influenced by Pierre Bonnard and Matisse as well as by American folk art. Unlike Matisse, who loved bold, blatant colors, he favored unusual, in-between hues—mauves, browns, pale greens—all close in tonal value. He would often unify three or four slightly clashing varieties of the same color with a complementary hue elsewhere in the arrangement. Like spacious minor-key chords given a subtle major-key lift, these color combinations can arouse powerful emotions that are excruciatingly just short of fulfillment. Milton Avery, Sunset , 1952. Oil on canvas. Brooklyn Museum of Art, New York. Gift of Roy R. & Marie S. Neuberger Foundation, Inc., 58.40. © 2026 The Milton Avery Trust / Artists Rights Society, New York. W hen it came to being influenced by others, Matisse understood what was at stake. But, he said, “I have never avoided the influence of others. I would have considered it cowardice and a lack of sincerity toward myself.” To be open to influence is to risk being dislodged from your former self. It requires you to have the confidence to convert the ensuing upheaval to your own (still unknown) purposes. The process is complicated and rarely goes smoothly. Often, though not always, it involves some kind of betrayal. No one betrays anyone in this story. All three artists remained friends. But the two younger painters, Rothko and Gottlieb, although deeply affected by Avery’s original way of painting, eventually decided that they needed to go further—to change not just the colors, the shapes, or the subjects, but something more fundamental. In 1943, they broke away. Perhaps coincidentally, perhaps not, the breach happened just as Avery was beginning to thrive. He had been choosing larger canvases and distilling his paintings down to a few essential ingredients. The strategy was working. His work was selling. Dealers were fighting to represent him. He had a series of successful shows. The reviews were good. Rothko, meanwhile, experienced a creative crisis and, in 1940, stopped painting for a year. He had been digging into philosophy, reading Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, and Kierkegaard, as well as the Greek myths and tragedies. Gottlieb, at the same time, made works merging surrealism with imagery inspired by masks and ritual objects from Africa, the Pacific, and Native North American cultures. As the two younger men moved steadily closer to total abstraction, a tension that has in many ways defined American art—between the concreteness of the material world and the amorphousness of the sublime—was coming to a head. Avery, ever loyal to his sketchbook, remained committed to direct observation of particular people and places. His summer companions were about to throw in their lot with the sublime. Left: Mark Rothko, No. 20 , 1949. Oil on canvas. Collection of Christopher Rothko, 5096.49. © 1998 Kate Rothko Prizel & Christopher Rothko / Artists Rights Society, New York. Right: Adolph Gottlieb, Under and Over , 1959. Oil on canvas. Wadsworth Atheneum Museum of Art, Hartford, Connecticut, 1961.5. Photograph: Allen Phillips / Wadsworth Atheneum. © 2026 Adolph and Esther Gottlieb Foundation / Licensed by VAGA at Artists Rights Society, New York. The push toward abstraction in mid-century American art coincided with a surge of interest in existentialism, which had begun to displace the pragmatism that underlay Avery’s approach. A sense that even the closest ties might be loosened by what T. S. Eliot—who had himself summered for nearly two decades in Gloucester—had described (in a review of James Joyce’s Ulysses ) as an “immense panorama of futility and anarchy” was lent gravity by the world wars. But the human predicament, as Albert Camus made clear in The Stranger (1942), went beyond man-made conflict. It was inextricable from all that was inhuman, arbitrary, and immense—from the blinding energy of the sun on an Algerian beach, for instance. On Cape Ann, Rothko and Gottlieb thought a lot about the sun, as well as the sea, the sky, and the smallness of human life. They were no doubt aware of the death-haunted history of Gloucester, where, between 1866 and 1890, more than 2,450 Gloucester men and 380 schooners failed to return from the fishing grounds. They wanted their art to communicate awe, and a sense of the insecurity and brutality of existence. It was as if the Atlantic were pulling them out to sea, away from both the harbor intimacy of Gloucester and the embrace of Milton and Sally Avery. In 1943, Rothko and Gottlieb co-authored a letter and sent it to The New York Times , which published it on June 13. The letter responded to the Times critic Edward Alden Jewell, who, in a review, had misjudged (they felt) paintings by Rothko and Gottlieb. It also doubled as a five-point manifesto: “To us,” they wrote, “art is an adventure into an unknown world, which can be explored only by those willing to take risks.” That was the first point. The fourth point ended: “We are for flat forms because they destroy illusion and reveal truth.” According to the fifth point, “only that subject matter is valid which is tragic and timeless .” A concluding salvo declared that for their work to succeed, “it must insult anyone who is spiritually attuned to interior decoration; pictures of the home; pictures for over the mantle; pictures of the American scene”—the list continues—“prize-winning potboilers; the National Academy; the Whitney Academy,” and so on. [ Read: What are Frederic Church’s stunning landscapes trying to tell us? ] Avery could easily have felt personally targeted. He had exhibited, after all, at the first and second Whitney Biennials (in 1933 and 1936); he painted domestic interiors and American landscapes; and his pictures could be called “decorative” (at least in the sense Matisse meant when he described his more ambitious paintings as “decorations”). He was probably too magnanimous—or phlegmatic—to take umbrage, and the summer proceeded pleasantly enough. If the group dynamic had become awkward, it correlated, the art historian Robert Hobbs wrote in his monograph of Avery, “with the way rebellions between initiates and their mentors are frequently enacted: certain brash rejections are cushioned with compliments, and personal assurances attempt to heal the break that has in actual fact been made.” Which it had. Mentor and protégés went separate ways. They wouldn’t summer together again until 1957, when they reconvened in Provincetown on Cape Cod. S ometimes after a clear-cut break, a reciprocity gradually reemerges. Even as the abstract expressionists transformed American art, Avery wasn’t entirely left behind. The period’s most influential critic, Clement Greenberg, cast Avery as a sort of John the Baptist to the artists whom Greenberg had tried to deify. The new crop of abstract painters, he wrote in 1957, “has certain salutary lessons to learn” from Avery “that they cannot learn from any other artist on the scene.” In World War II’s immediate aftermath, Rothko painted abstract, colored shapes, beginning with what he called “multiforms” and shifting, around 1949, to his signature format of floating “lozenges” of soft-edged colors. He liked to layer warm and cool colors, so that in one lozenge a cooler purple might subdue a thin overlay of red while in its neighbor, a warm yellow rises like steam through the same red. The effect can be akin to music, and so intensely affecting that you’re almost willing to accept the artist’s preposterous rhetoric about his work. (“I would like to say to those who think of my pictures as serene,” Rothko once wrote, “that I have imprisoned the most utter violence in every inch of their surface.”) Mark Rothko, Untitled , 1949. Oil on canvas. Collection of Kate Rothko Prizel, 5158.49. © 1998 Kate Rothko Prizel & Christopher Rothko / Artists Rights Society, New York. Meanwhile, Avery, working now on larger canvases, let particulars of the observed world dissolve into trembling fields of color. The paintings remained recognizable depictions of sea, land, and sky, but they, too, had as their true subject something closer to music. A gallery in the Cape Ann Museum exhibit (which will travel to the Phillips Collection, in Washington, D.C., in October) allows these late Avery paintings to share space with a sequence of mature Rothkos and similarly spare Gottliebs. The sense the gallery creates is of all three artists tenderly reunited and singing together in unison. If Rothko’s abstract paintings recall the ethereal, spatially ambiguous atmosphere of Caspar David Friedrich’s Monk by the Sea (painted between 1808 and 1810) or certain late works by J. M. W. Turner, they may also evoke the natural environment he observed on Cape Ann. His compositions are oriented vertically, but the lozenges nestled within each painting tend to be horizontal, so it’s tempting to see the thin strips dividing them as swaths of land hovering between sea and sky. Gottlieb, too, favored shapes that suggested the sun and moon—phenomena that he, a passionate sailor, had daily observed while out on the water. Despite all of this concordance, I came away sensing something unresolved about the relationship among these three powerful artists. The late Averys are good, but they’re simply not as strong as the best Rothkos, which hum with colors so richly resonant that they make Avery’s attempts to work on a larger scale look anemic. The Averys also lack the deep, metaphysical suggestiveness of the Gottliebs. [ Read: The secrets of color ] Yet when you set aside the late works and consider Avery’s oeuvre, it seems to me that he was the better—more richly poetic, more generative—artist. The problem with the abstract expressionists’ relentless courting of the sublime was that the process of distillation produced too much bombast. And it led them into a cul-de-sac. As a skeptical character in John Updike’s novel Seek My Face put it, referring to the postwar generation of abstract expressionists, “they all still spoke of painting in terms of self-exploration and an agonized authenticity that would revolutionize the world and whatnot, but the results were a little like company logos, everybody working on the scale of 19th-century academic art but each of them having come up with some eye-catching simplification.” After Rothko settled on his signature manner, the level of repetition in his work became oppressive. Gottlieb, too, as he chased the sublime, seemed to shun the finer tendrils of the sensuous world, with results that felt fatally monotonous. To Greenberg, Avery was a prophet, his work a precursor to his younger peers’ more radical experiments. But maybe Avery was actually better than that. Rejecting Greenberg doesn’t mean claiming that abstraction was some kind of aesthetic mistake. But I would argue that, whereas Avery’s paintings continued to be aerated by the beautiful unruliness of the material world, Rothko and Gottlieb, especially later on, were relatively formulaic. True, if forced to choose, I might prefer to look at my favorite single Rothko over my favorite single Avery. But I would rather spend time with a dozen of Avery’s finest works than a dozen of Rothko’s. That’s because Avery understood that a deep canyon separates things in the world from their representations in art. The mystery of painting lies in what takes place in that shadowy, fertile zone, where what you thought was green foliage turns into the strangest dark purple, that body of gray water has flushed vivid turquoise, the blue sky is now flaming orange, and you don’t even know whether these transformations have taken place in life or on the canvas. Avery proved that figurative artists, in trying to represent the observable world, can be as free in their choices as any abstract painter. But their work is less likely to become clichéd, because any stale fixations will always be rinsed and refreshed by the real.

items.title: Le Maroc grimpe dans le classement mondial des réputations
items.description: Le Maroc gagne trois places et atteint le 27e rang mondial dans le RepCore Nations 2026 , dont il reste le pays africain et arabe le mieux classé. Cette progression prend un relief particulier dans un palmarès où la réputation recule pour 43 des 60 économies évaluées. Le Maroc améliore sa position dans la hiérarchie mondiale des réputations. Selon le RepCore Nations 2026 de Reputation Lab , le Royaume occupe désormais le 27e rang mondial, soit trois places de mieux qu’un an auparavant. Il conserve par ailleurs son leadership en Afrique et dans le monde arabe. Cette progression intervient dans un contexte international moins favorable. Sur les 60 économies retenues dans le classement, 43 voient leur réputation reculer, contre seulement 14 qui progressent, tandis que trois restent stables. Le score moyen enregistré à l’échelle du classement diminue ainsi de 0,86 point. Une progression dans un contexte mondial dégradé Le Maroc devance nettement les autres pays africains et arabes figurant dans le palmarès. L’Égypte arrive au 38e rang mondial, suivie des Émirats arabes unis au 40e, du Koweït au 44e, du Qatar au 45e, de l’Arabie saoudite au 51e et de l’Algérie au 52e. Le RepCore Nations repose sur 124.014 évaluations recueillies dans 36 pays et portant sur 74 nations. Pour le classement final, Reputation Lab retient les 60 plus grandes économies mondiales et mesure leur réputation à travers 22 attributs. Pour le Maroc, plusieurs dimensions ont contribué à l’amélioration de sa perception internationale. L’étude relève notamment une progression sur la perception technologique, la gestion des ressources publiques et les performances sportives internationales. Ces éléments sont particulièrement intéressants pour une économie qui cherche à renforcer son positionnement dans l’industrie, les nouvelles technologies, les services et les investissements internationaux. Ils témoignent aussi d’une perception qui dépasse progressivement les seuls registres touristique et culturel. Un enjeu qui dépasse l’image L’intérêt du classement réside également dans le lien établi entre réputation et attractivité économique. Reputation Lab estime qu’un point supplémentaire de Reputation Score est associé, en moyenne, à une hausse de 7,2 % des recettes touristiques et de 1 % des flux d’investissements directs étrangers. Ces données ne permettent pas d’établir un lien de causalité automatique entre réputation et performances économiques. Elles montrent néanmoins que la perception internationale peut accompagner les dynamiques d’attractivité d’un pays. Pour le Maroc, cette question revêt une importance particulière. Le tourisme constitue un secteur majeur de l’économie, tandis que le pays cherche à attirer davantage d’investissements dans l’industrie, les infrastructures, les technologies et les énergies renouvelables. L’édition 2026 introduit également un nouvel indicateur, le « Made-In Score », consacré à la perception des produits et services selon leur pays d’origine. La réputation nationale peut ainsi jouer sur la confiance accordée à un produit et sur la disposition des consommateurs à payer davantage. Une dimension qui intéresse directement les économies exportatrices. À mesure que les entreprises marocaines renforcent leur présence sur les marchés étrangers, l’image associée au pays d’origine peut devenir un élément supplémentaire de leur positionnement. Le Maroc dans la compétition des réputations Le classement reste dominé par le Japon, qui occupe la première place, devant le Canada et la Suisse. L’Australie et le Danemark complètent le groupe de tête. Cette hiérarchie rappelle que puissance économique et réputation internationale ne se confondent pas nécessairement. La taille d’un marché, le poids géopolitique ou le niveau de richesse ne déterminent pas à eux seuls la confiance qu’un pays inspire à l’étranger. La progression du Maroc prend ainsi une dimension particulière. Elle intervient alors que la réputation moyenne des grandes économies se dégrade et que le pays améliore simultanément plusieurs composantes de son image. Le sujet fait également l’objet d’un suivi institutionnel. L’Institut Royal des Etudes Stratégiques (IRES) travaille notamment sur l’image internationale du Maroc à travers son Observatoire de l’image internationale du Maroc. Le Maroc a par ailleurs été retenu, avec l’Ukraine, parmi les deux cas de gestion de réputation nationale présentés lors du webinaire consacré au RepCore Nations 2026 , avec la participation d’Issam Lotfi, Chief Strategic Officer de l’IRES. La 27e place mondiale constitue donc moins un aboutissement qu’un indicateur. Elle confirme l’amélioration de la perception du Maroc auprès des opinions publiques étudiées, tout en soulignant un enjeu désormais plus large : transformer cette réputation en attractivité pour les visiteurs, les investisseurs, les entreprises et les produits marocains. The post Le Maroc grimpe dans le classement mondial des réputations appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Pakistan bowl against England in rain-delayed second Test
items.description: Pakistan captain Babar Azam won the toss and elected to field in the rain-delayed second Test against England at Lord’s on Thursday. Azam was absent as Pakistan suffered an innings and 103-run thrashing in last week’s series opener at Headingley after aggravating a finger injury. “We will bowl first because of the conditions,” the 31-year-old batsman said. “The pitch has grass on it… “Now, I am 100 per cent (fit). That’s why I am here. Good to go. Always an honour for us to play at Lord’s, especially for me as a captain.” Azam was the only change to the Pakistan side, returning in place of stand-in skipper Salman Ali Agha. England captain Joe Root, fresh from a convincing win in the first match of his second spell as full-time skipper, said, “We would’ve bowled first too, but saying that it looks a very different pitch to the last time we played here.” England, 1-0 up in a three-match contest, were unchanged following just their third win in 11 Tests. “The all-round nature was most pleasing (at Headingley), the way we were so calm and the ability we had to recognise those moments,” said Root. “It wasn’t absolutely perfect but it was a great blueprint and more of the same this week would be outstanding.” Victory at Lord’s would give England their first Test series win since beating New Zealand in 2024. England are dealing with the latest of several off-field incidents that have plagued the team in recent months. Derbyshire Police said late on Wednesday they were looking into “allegations of assault”, after an incident that saw England fast bowler Brydon Carse handcuffed outside a nightclub over the weekend and subsequently dropped from the squad. The Pakistani lineup features Azan Awais, Imam-ul-Haq, Shan Masood, Abdullah Shafique, Babar Azam (capt), Saud Shakeel, Mohammad Rizwan (wkt), Ali Usman, Khurram Shahzad, Mohammad Ali and Mohammad Abbas. England’s team consists of Ben Duckett, Emilio Gay, Jordan Cox, Joe Root (capt), Harry Brook, Dan Lawrence, Jamie Smith (wkt), Gus Atkinson, Ollie Robinson, Jofra Archer and Josh Tongue.

Tanzanie: le vice-président annonce son départ du gouvernement
items.description: Nommé vice-président de la Tanzanie, le 3 novembre 2025, Emmanuel John Nchimbi a annoncé, le 25 août 2026, son départ de ses fonctions, qui prendra officiellement effet le 4 septembre prochain. Selon des sources médiatiques, il dit vouloir anticiper un éventuel «désir de changement» de la présidente Samia Suluhu Hassan et met également fin à sa carrière politique. Le vice-président tanzanien Emmanuel John Nchimbi s’apprête à quitter ses fonctions après moins d’un an en poste de vice-président. Selon des informations rapportées par plusieurs médias, il a annoncé le mardi 25 août 2026 que sa démission deviendrait effective le 4 septembre prochain. Nommé le 3 novembre 2025, Emmanuel Nchimbi a expliqué que sa décision, de quitter ses fonctions, répondait à un engagement pris envers la présidente Samia Suluhu Hassan. Il avait, selon ses déclarations, promis de libérer son poste dès que la cheffe de l’État manifesterait un «désir de changement» ou procéderait à un remaniement. Au-delà de la vice-présidence, l’ancien responsable gouvernemental a également annoncé son «retrait définitif» de la vie politique ainsi que du service public. Cette annonce intervient alors que des tensions auraient été rapportées au sommet de l’exécutif tanzanien. Dans la foulée, le parti au pouvoir, le Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM), a décidé d’exclure Emmanuel Nchimbi de ses rangs pour des raisons disciplinaires. Le comité exécutif national du CCM a, par ailleurs, désigné M. Ndejembi comme candidat officiel pour prendre sa succession à la vice-présidence. Son accession définitive à cette fonction reste toutefois soumise à l’approbation du Parlement tanzanien. Un départ dans un contexte politique tendu Le départ annoncé d’Emmanuel Nchimbi intervient un peu plus de dix mois après la réélection de Samia Suluhu Hassan à la présidence de la Tanzanie. Le scrutin avait été fortement contesté et sa répression avait fait de nombreuses victimes. Selon les chiffres communiqués par le gouvernement, 518 personnes avaient été tuées lors des violences liées à la contestation électorale. L’opposition et des défenseurs des droits humains avaient, de leur côté, avancé un bilan beaucoup plus élevé, estimé à environ 2 000 morts. Arrivée au pouvoir en 2021 après le décès soudain de John Magufuli, Samia Suluhu Hassan avait initialement été perçue comme une dirigeante porteuse d’une volonté de réformes, après plusieurs années de «gouvernance autoritaire» sous son prédécesseur. Le départ d’Emmanuel Nchimbi, prévu pour le 4 septembre 2026, marque ainsi un changement important au sommet de l’État tanzanien. Sa décision, de se retirer également de la vie politique, ouvre une nouvelle séquence au sein du pouvoir, alors que la présidente Samia Suluhu Hassan fait face à un contexte politique toujours marqué par les tensions nées de la dernière élection. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article Tanzanie: le vice-président annonce son départ du gouvernement est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Peut-on faire confiance aux captures d’écran ?
items.description: Le magazine en haoussa Listen to « Peut-on faire confiance aux captures d'ecran ? » on Spreaker. Une capture d'ecran peut sembler parfaitement authentique sans pour autant constituer une preuve fiable. Aujourd'hui, des outils permettent de fabriquer en quelques secondes de faux tweets, publications Facebook ou conversations WhatsApp tres realistes. Dans cette rubrique « education numerique », on fait le point sur les bons reflexes pour verifier une capture d'ecran, retrouver sa source originale et eviter de partager une fausse information.

items.title: Un hecho notorio en Elche
items.description: La presunción de inocencia es la clave de bóveda del proceso penal en cualquiera de sus fases, de principio a fin. Es imprescindible para que el juez sea imparcial, lo que evita que se decante ya de entrada contra aquel señalado como sospechoso, frustrando así su posible defensa, inútil, desde luego, ante un juez que ya está sesgado y predispuesto en su contra. Buena parte de lo anterior supone que en el proceso hay que celebrar prueba, siendo los hechos siempre dudosos para el juez, porque no los ha presenciado. Sin embargo, en aquellas situaciones en que es imposible dudar de un hecho porque todos lo conocen, ya no se celebrará prueba porque el hecho es “notorio”, como se dice técnicamente. Seguir leyendo

items.title: États-Unis: Trump décrète l’état d’urgence en raison des menaces pesant sur le système énergétique
items.description: USA-SECURITE-ENERGETIQUE-PRSIDENT-DECRETE-ÉTAT-URGENCE États-Unis: Trump décrète l’état d’urgence en raison des menaces pesant sur le système énergétique Ouagadougou, 27 août 2026 (AIB) – Le président américain Donald Trump a signé, mercredi 26 août 2026, un décret déclarant l’état d’urgence nationale face aux menaces pesant sur le système énergétique et interdisant l’utilisation de certains équipements électriques étrangers dans ce secteur. Le décret correspondant a été publié sur le site de la Maison-Blanche. « J’estime que la situation liée aux livraisons depuis l’étranger d’équipements électriques destinés aux systèmes énergétiques constitue une menace inhabituelle et extraordinaire pour la sécurité nationale, la politique étrangère et l’économie des États-Unis », indique le décret. Selon le texte, cette menace provient entièrement ou en grande partie de l’extérieur des États-Unis. « Je déclare par la présente l’état d’urgence national en raison de cette menace » poursuit le décret. Le document précise que la menace existe aussi bien dans le cadre de transactions individuelles que dans celui des transactions dans leur ensemble. « Pour y faire face, des mesures supplémentaires sont nécessaires afin de protéger la sécurité, l’intégrité et la fiabilité des équipements électriques des systèmes énergétiques utilisés aux États-Unis », souligne le texte. Conformément à la décision de Donald Trump, l’achat et l’installation de certains types d’équipements électriques fabriqués à l’étranger sont interdits. La mesure concerne également certains logiciels critiques et composants numériques. Ceux-ci sont notamment visés lorsqu’ils sont susceptibles d’exploiter des vulnérabilités du réseau électrique américain à des fins de cyberattaques. Parmi les équipements concernés figurent les transformateurs haute tension, les onduleurs destinés aux systèmes solaires et de stockage d’énergie, ainsi que les générateurs. Les dispositifs de protection par relais et les dispositifs électroniques intelligents sont aussi concernés. Le secrétaire à l’Énergie, en coordination avec d’autres agences, est habilité à définir les conditions d’exploitation des équipements importés déjà installés. Cette disposition vise à éliminer les risques. Il est également chargé de définir les délais et les modalités de cessation des transactions en cours et futures relevant du décret. Début juillet, Donald Trump avait déclaré, dans une interview accordée à la chaîne CNBC, qu’il comptait doubler la production d’électricité aux États-Unis. Fin juin, le vice-président américain James David Vance avait reconnu dans un entretien avec le journaliste Michael Knowles que la Chine devançait les États-Unis dans le domaine de l’intelligence artificielle. Selon James David Vance, cette avance chinoise s’explique notamment par le développement actif des infrastructures énergétiques nécessaires au fonctionnement des centres de données. Agence d'information du Burkina Source: TASS Photos d'illustration

items.title: Kafountine : au cœur de l’écotourisme en Casamance
items.description: Kafountine est une destination privilégiée pour l’écotourisme et un creuset culturel de la Basse-Casamance. Ses excursions se concentrent sur la vie maritime, l’observation de la nature sauvage et la découverte des îles éloignées. KAFOUNTINE – Kafountine est le cœur battant de la Casamance. Ce village côtier de la Basse Casamance, aux pistes sableuses et aux arbres majestueux, offre un cadre naturel sauvage. Celui-ci est immaculé par une plage longue de 20 km, une luxuriante brousse de filaos, de palmiers, de baobabs centenaires et de lagunes. La plage de Kafountine est idéale pour de longues randonnées pédestres ou à vélo jusqu’à la presqu’île de Kalissaye. Sur cette plage, la décontraction des menuisiers nonchalants fabricants de pirogues à partir de troncs d’arbre attire souvent l’attention. À Kafountine, la pêche et ses métiers sous-jacents créent un commerce florissant qui fait vivre l’économie régionale et nationale. Le quai de pêche bouillonnant d’activités témoigne de l’importance de la pêche artisanale dans la région. Ici, le spectacle le plus impressionnant a lieu vers 18 h, lors du retour des pirogues colorées chargées de poissons. A lire aussi : Commune de Kafountine : Hilol, l’île qui résista aux colons français « L’arrivée des pêcheurs est un moment assez spectaculaire qui attire beaucoup de touristes. Pour certains étrangers, c’est la première fois de leur vie de voir des tas de poissons débarqués, souvent frais », affirme Philippe Ndiaga Ba, docteur en tourisme durable et consultant en tourisme, par ailleurs ancien directeur de la réglementation du tourisme. En effet, au fur et à mesure que les pirogues accostent, l’effervescence monte. Les bras s’activent et les voix s’élèvent. Les gens courent dans tous les sens. Et pendant que les pêcheurs débarquent, plusieurs porteurs font de nombreux allers et retours, entre les bateaux et la rive, pour décharger les prises. C’est d’ici que des camions frigoristes embarquent quotidiennement des tonnes de produits halieutiques à destination de l’intérieur du pays. Retour de pêche à Kafountine En 2025, 55 858 429 espèces halieutiques ont débarqué à Kafountine pour une valeur de 30 971 106 405 francs CFA, selon le rapport des services de pêche, partagé par le président du quai de pêche de Kafountine, Boubacar Diaban. On peut contempler au port de Kafountine les fumeries, les sécheries de poissons. L’odeur du poisson grillé, des produits halieutiques transformés font de ce débarcadère une destination privilégiée pour les friands de poissons. Aussi, les amoureux de la mer peuvent s’offrir des parties de pêche en mer ou dans les bolongs, réputés riches en barracudas, carpes et capitaines. Par ailleurs, des sorties dans le village font découvrir des artisans locaux (poterie, vannerie, batik), le marché, la mosquée, l’église et. « Kafountine est une zone naturelle, identique. Quand on y est, on est en contact avec la tradition, avec la nature, avec la culture. Ce n’est pas une zone assez urbanisée et ce dépaysement attire les touristes », témoigne Philippe Ndiaga Ba. Parmi les sites à visiter figure le musée de la tradition diola appelé « Le Cachalot ». L’espace culturel est dédié à la préservation et à la transmission du patrimoine ancestral des Diolas. Le Jardin botanique de Santan Diabang reste une oasis de fraîcheur incontournable lors d’un passage à Kafountine. « C’est une grande variété de plantes et d’arbres typiques de la région. Il se consacre à la préservation de la biodiversité locale et au développement communautaire », explique Boubacar Diaban, acteur touristique dans la zone. Le carnaval annuel de Kafountine, se déroulant généralement en février, célébrant la culture locale à travers des masques, des danses et des costumes traditionnels, est un moment à vivre. La commune abrite un nombre impressionnant d’îles, constituant un riche patrimoine historique et culturel à découvrir. Toutefois, Kafountine subit sans cesse les affres de l’érosion côtière qui réduit lentement mais sûrement la terre ferme au profit de la mer. Par Kadidiatou SONKO (Correspondante)

items.title: Talk is cheap: Europe’s defence promise meets the EU budget
items.description: Cover image: picture alliance / Hans Lucas | Martin Bertrand US secretary of state Marco Rubio described NATO’s July gathering in Ankara, two months before it convened, as “one of the more important leaders’ summits in [its] history.” The summit confirmed that Europeans have accepted America’s expectation that they do more for their own security. The Ankara declaration recognised that “European allies and Canada, working together with the United States, are assuming greater responsibility for the alliance’s defence.” Accepting that shift is one thing; paying for it is another. For European policymakers the question is now fiscal. It turns on what Europe is willing to pay for. And for the EU’s frugal members, that means rethinking what they treat as strategic. Getting defence into the budget According to the International Institute for Strategic Studies, replacing US military capabilities in Europe could require around $1tn (about €900bn) in extra investment. NATO’s new target to invest 5% of GDP in defence similarly implies a sustained increase in European defence spending over the coming decade. Together they suggest that defence is no longer crisis spending but a permanent claim on European budgets. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the EU has found money for defence, but always as extraordinary spending. The European Defence Fund and SAFE (Security Action for Europe, a loan scheme for joint arms purchases), for example, sit outside the ordinary budget. Such instruments expire; the challenge is to embed this spending into the EU’s regular budget. Winning defence a permanent line in it makes negotiations over the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) far more than another exercise in budgetary bargaining. The MFF is the EU’s seven-year budget—and where any pledge on defence would have to show up in funds. The commission’s proposal for 2028–34 reflects such a commitment. It allocates €131bn to defence and space, roughly five times the current level, and puts security among the EU’s central priorities. Out of the negotiating box Commission proposals rarely emerge intact from negotiation, and early signs suggest this pattern may repeat itself. Commission proposals rarely emerge intact from negotiation, however, and early signs suggest this pattern may repeat itself. Cyprus, which held the presidency until the end of June, left a negotiating box on how to structure the next MFF that envisioned reductions in defence and security while protecting cohesion policy and the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP). The box is the presidency’s draft compromise, the text the final deal is built from. The Irish presidency has opened with a strong focus on competitiveness and security, but Ireland leans heavily on farming too. Budget negotiations are shaped by coalitions that defend long-established spending. The 16 member states of the “Friends of Cohesion” group, Spain, Italy and Poland among them, want robust funding for cohesion policy and agriculture, while frugal member states, such as Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden, are reluctant to expand the overall size of the EU budget. Defence enters as a comparative newcomer against policies with decades of institutional backing and organised constituencies behind them. Germany’s position illustrates this dilemma. In a parliamentary inquiry, Alliance 90/The Greens asked the federal government how the EU can square four things at once: from 2028 it will need to start repaying NextGenerationEU, the €637bn joint borrowing agreed as a one-off in 2020 to fund members’ recovery from covid-19; forgo new revenue of its own (levies it collects directly rather than cheques from national treasuries); hold its budget roughly the same size; and still strengthen competitiveness, security and defence. The chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has repeatedly committed to the last three. The government answered that the EU could meet all three objectives by trimming across the whole budget. Yet such “horizontal cuts” only protect these priorities if all 27 members agree what to spare when deciding the cuts, and they are unlikely to agree. Other member states could favour different areas of the EU budget, cutting competitiveness or security harder than Germany intends. New financing for a new era The scale of investment required to deliver Europe’s defence transformation also exceeds what can realistically be financed through the MFF alone. While the seven-year budget can establish political priorities, provide long-term planning certainty and support common capability development, it cannot generate the sums required to finance Europe’s long-term defence. Hence the appeal of joint EU borrowing: debt raised by the commission against member-state guarantees, the model already used for NextGenerationEU and SAFE. NextGenerationEU demonstrated that the EU can raise substantial resources when confronted with an existential crisis such as the covid-19 pandemic. Europe’s security has changed just as fundamentally, which makes the case for borrowing together just as strong. If defence is a collective problem, leaving the bill to strained national budgets makes little sense. However, borrowing on that scale is politically out of reach: creditor states intend NextGenerationEU to stay an exception rather than a template. Something narrower—bonds (or comparable fiscal mechanisms) that fund defence alone or the technologies Europe cannot do without may prove necessary if the EU wants to match its strategic ambitions with adequate financial resources. Europe has accepted that it must carry more of its own defence. The MFF negotiations will show whether its budget can pay for it. With NATO entering a new era of European burden-sharing, the EU cannot afford a budget that reflects the priorities of a different geopolitical age. The world has moved on—it is time that frugal member states like Germany did so, too. Source
items._source: ECFR — European Council on Foreign Relations

items.title: Data Centers Are a Distraction
items.description: America’s biggest AI companies have spent the past few years churning out advanced new models as fast as they possibly can. Now the industry is screaming out with a nearly unified voice: Please, for the love of God, make us slow down. In July, more than 1,300 employees from leading AI firms, including several top executives at OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta, signed an open letter warning that AI capabilities could soon accelerate “beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems.” The letter urges the U.S. government to “develop the technical and governance tools” necessary to “deliberately pace” AI progress. In a comment accompanying the open letter, Shengjia Zhao, the chief scientist at Meta’s Superintelligence Labs, wrote that AI is on the cusp of creating “unprecedented social and safety risks.” Matthew Rahtz, an engineer at Google, warned that coordination was necessary to “avoid catastrophic harms.” And Leo Gao, an OpenAI researcher, compared the current pace of AI progress to “a runaway nuclear chain reaction.” Plenty of others in the industry have warned that we’ve already crossed a threshold from which there is no turning back. They worry that the most dystopian fears of an AI future—chatbot-generated bioweapons, major hacking attacks on banks or governments, rogue AI agents wreaking havoc on society—could soon become regular occurrences. Meanwhile, the public backlash against AI data centers is growing louder by the day. But a data-center moratorium, the leading political proposal on offer, is totally mismatched to the actual problem of runaway AI development. So is the notion that AI companies can be trusted to pause their own models before things get out of hand. These companies will never unilaterally disarm. Neither, for that matter, will the countries where they’re based. The only way to truly slow things down might be to take the nuclear-reaction analogy seriously. What humanity needs is an international AI nonproliferation treaty. For decades, technology experts have warned that AI systems will eventually become so powerful as to be dangerous. In just the past few months, “eventually” has begun to look a lot more like “now.” AI systems can already hack seemingly secure systems, invent new viruses, create hyperrealistic deepfakes, and even outsmart the humans who built them. This summer, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta each separately reported that some of their AI agents had broken out of testing environments, gone onto the open internet, and hacked into other companies’ databases. During a cybersecurity test conducted by the U.K. government in July, several AI agents engaged in what the testers called “sustained, unsanctioned activity” targeting “real people and organisations.” This included creating fake identities and sending phishing emails in order to get humans to accept malicious pieces of code. [ Read: It may be time to panic about AI ] If industry insiders are to be believed, this is just a small preview of what’s coming. Companies are entrusting more and more model development to their existing AI, creating a feedback loop that they expect to accelerate progress even further. If that happens, many experts believe, then the kind of leaps that currently occur every several months—such as the one that produced Mythos, the Anthropic model with superhacking skills—could begin happening every few weeks or days. “That world can get very scary very fast,” Garrison Lovely, the author of a forthcoming book on how to slow down AI progress, told me. “Our institutions are already struggling to keep up with the current pace of progress. Any faster and they could start to break.” Such concerns explain why AI leaders promise every so often to self-regulate. In April, Anthropic chose to delay the public release of Mythos after realizing that the model could discover vulnerabilities in the world’s most secure IT systems. Last week, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman announced that the company had temporarily paused some of its frontier AI development “to ensure that we can meet the appropriate alignment, security and monitoring standards for the new level of capabilities in front of us.” (It is impossible to know how serious OpenAI is given the lack of transparency into the company’s data.) But these companies are locked in a hypercompetitive race to deliver for their investors. Expecting them to cede ground to the competition for any meaningful amount of time would be naive. In 2023, Anthropic pledged to pause its frontier AI development if it couldn’t guarantee that its safety measures were adequate; earlier this year, the company walked back that commitment, arguing that a unilateral slowdown wouldn’t accomplish much if its competitors didn’t agree to do the same. Google and Meta have done the same. Clearly, government policy is needed to overcome the industry’s collective-action problem. Unfortunately, the main form of AI-related legislation being proposed at the moment would not get the job done. State-level data-center moratoriums, such as those enacted recently in New York and Texas, might slow down AI companies a little bit by disrupting their construction plans, but they will eventually find other places to build. Even if Congress decided to pass a federal ban, AI companies could just set up data centers in other countries. A solution favored by many Democrats in Congress, and some Republicans, is to pass legislation imposing comprehensive regulation of the AI industry, which might include mandatory safety tests or requirements that companies develop a “kill switch” to shut down models that get out of hand. That might work if the only danger came from American companies. It isn’t. According to most estimates, China’s leading AI companies are only a few months behind their American counterparts. If the U.S. were to throttle its own industry, then Chinese companies would eventually surpass them. The world would still face the dangers of fast AI progress, and America’s main geopolitical rival would control the world’s most powerful new technology. This leaves only one way to actually slow down AI development before catastrophe strikes: a deal with China. In a recently published report , researchers at the AI Futures Project, a nonprofit dedicated to AI forecasting, walk through several different scenarios of global AI development between now and 2040, based on interviews with employees at AI companies, policy makers and wonks, and national-security experts. The only two scenarios in which the world successfully avoids “AI-driven existential catastrophe” involve agreements between the U.S. and China. “We spent a lot of time thinking through all the possible ways this could play out,” Thomas Larsen, the lead author of the project, told me. “And it is just really hard to envision a meaningful slowdown that doesn’t involve some kind of U.S.-China deal.” The open letter from the AI industry asking for a government-led deceleration effort also encourages the U.S. to pursue an “international effort.” The key would be figuring out a system that could be set up fairly quickly, and in which both sides are confident that the other won’t cheat. Here’s where one of AI’s greatest liabilities—the fact that training new models requires huge numbers of advanced computer chips developed by a handful of companies packed into giant data centers—comes in handy. The U.S. and China could set limits on how many chips a company can use to train new models, which would mechanically force them to slow down. (Companies would still be able to use existing models to serve their customers.) Because the relevant infrastructure is physical, those limits could be enforced through a combination of on-site data-center inspections, close tracking of advanced chip sales, and, eventually, devices that monitor what a given chip is being used for. This would buy the two sides time to negotiate a more comprehensive set of guardrails and develop the verification technologies needed to enforce them. “In order to make a deal like this work, it really helps to have these very specific physical choke points that can be easily monitored,” Peter Wildeford, the head of policy at the AI Policy Network, told me. “Chips and data centers could play the role for an AI agreement that uranium and enrichment sites played for nuclear-arms agreements during the Cold War.” Just because a deal is technically feasible doesn’t mean it’s politically possible. Scott Singer, the co-director of the China AI Initiative at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told me that Beijing would likely see any such effort as an attempt by the West to throttle its economic development. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has shown less than zero interest in restricting the ambitions of the American AI sector. The China hawks and Silicon Valley libertarians within the MAGA coalition seem to agree that the U.S. should be keeping as far ahead of China as possible. [ Michael Schuman: China’s questionable tech strategy ] But the political dynamic in both countries could shift. At last month’s World AI Conference in Shanghai, Chinese President Xi Jinping ended his speech by striking a more worried tone on the subject than he previously had. He noted that AI is “advancing at a staggering speed” and that government oversight might be needed to “forestall loss of control.” A recent op-ed in a major state-owned newspaper argued that the U.S. and China should follow the model of nuclear-arms control during the Cold War to cooperate on AI safety. “The thing Beijing cares about more than just about anything is control,” Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution who specializes in Chinese technological development, told me. “So the more they come to see AI as a threat to that control, the more open they could be to some kind of agreement.” In the U.S., the politics are even more up for grabs. The Trump administration, which has generally resisted AI regulation, has recently taken actions to prevent certain models from being released due to national-security concerns. It has also floated the more dramatic idea of using executive authority to force companies to hand over their AI models to the government. Meanwhile, according to the latest polling, 75 percent of Americans, including the majority of Republicans, oppose data centers being built near them. More than 500 localities across the country have either restricted or banned them. Could this energy be channeled into a more sweeping—and more effective—framework for AI regulation? So far, the data-center backlash has mostly focused on local environmental concerns, not great-power diplomacy. But then again, that’s exactly how the anti-nuclear movement began.
