items.title: Immersion patriotique 2026 : « La jeunesse ne doit pas être un simple témoin de l’histoire, elle doit en être un acteur engagé » (Porte-parole des appelés à l’immersion)
items.description: La deuxième édition de l’Immersion patriotique obligatoire (IPO) s’est achevée ce jeudi 27 août 2026 sur l’ensemble du territoire national. À cette occasion, la porte-parole des appelés, Océane Tiendrébéogo, a invité ses camarades à ne pas rester de simples spectateurs de l’histoire, mais à devenir des acteurs pleinement engagés dans la construction du Burkina Faso. « La jeunesse ne doit pas être un simple témoin de l’histoire, elle doit en être un acteur engagé », a déclaré la porte-parole des appelés, Océane Tiendrébéogo dans son discours de clôture. Elle a précisé que l’immersion avait permis aux participants de renforcer leur compréhension de la citoyenneté et de leur responsabilité envers la Nation. 65 000 appelés à l'immersion effectuent leur sortie après 1 mois de formation Venus d’horizons divers, les jeunes appelés ont affirmé achever cette session avec une conviction renforcée quant à leur rôle dans l’édification d’un Burkina Faso prospère. Pour Océane Tiendrébéogo, le patriotisme ne saurait toutefois se réduire aux discours ou aux déclarations d’intention. Il relève avant tout de comportements quotidiens. Au cours de leur immersion, les participants ont été sensibilisés à plusieurs valeurs jugées essentielles à la consolidation du vivre-ensemble et de la cohésion nationale. Le respect des aînés, la discipline, la protection des biens publics, le travail bien fait, l’honnêteté, la solidarité et le sens du sacrifice ont notamment été mis en avant. Océane Tiendrébéogo, a également insisté sur l’importance de la connaissance de l’histoire et de la diversité des communautés composant le Burkina Faso. Par ailleurs, les jeunes ont été informés des défis sécuritaires, économiques et sociaux auxquels le pays est confronté. Autant de difficultés qui, selon leur porte-parole, ne doivent pas mener au découragement, mais plutôt renforcer la détermination de la jeunesse à servir la Nation « avec courage, intégrité et dévouement ». S’adressant au Président du Faso, la porte-parole a relayé l’un des enseignements majeurs retenus durant la formation : le Baccalauréat ne doit pas être perçu comme une simple réussite académique, mais comme une responsabilité envers la Nation. À l’issue de l’immersion, les jeunes appelés ont pris plusieurs engagements solennels. Ce sont respecter les institutions de la République, aimer davantage leur pays, contribuer à sa protection, promouvoir l’unité nationale et servir leurs communautés avec solidarité et responsabilité. Océane Tiendrébéogo a également adressé, au nom des participants, des remerciements au coordinateur national de l’IPO, aux encadreurs, aux instructeurs, aux Forces de défense et de sécurité ainsi qu’aux différentes forces vives ayant contribué au bon déroulement de la session. Pour les jeunes appelés, la fin de l’IPO ne constitue pas un aboutissement, mais le début d’un engagement citoyen appelé à se poursuivre bien au-delà du cadre de la formation. « La clôture de notre session d’immersion patriotique obligatoire marque le début d’une mission », a affirmé la porte-parole, appelant ses camarades à incarner au quotidien l’exemplarité citoyenne. Elle a défendu l’idée d’un « citoyen nouveau », caractérisé par son attachement à la vérité, à la discipline et au travail au service de la patrie, et capable de faire passer l’intérêt collectif avant les considérations personnelles. En guise de conclusion, Océane Tiendrébéogo, au nom des jeunes appelés de l’IPO 2026, a pris un engagement solennel devant le Président du Faso, le peuple burkinabè et l’histoire. Les participants ont promis de servir le Burkina Faso « avec honneur, discipline et détermination », de placer la patrie au-dessus de leurs intérêts personnels et de défendre sa dignité et sa souveraineté. Ils se sont également engagés à être des citoyens responsables, courageux et solidaires, à respecter les lois et les institutions, et à combattre la haine, la division et la désinformation, présentées comme autant de menaces pour l’unité nationale. « Nous serons les sentinelles de l’esprit patriotique », a promis la porte-parole, avant de conclure par un appel à porter haut les couleurs du Burkina Faso. Chaque Immergés a reçu le Manifeste de la RPP Rappelons que selon le Coordonnateur national de l'immersion patriotique obligatoire, chacun des 65 000 appelés que compte cette édition de l'immersion patriotique obligatoire, repartira avec un exemplaire du manifeste de la RPP. Lire aussi : Immersion patriotique 2026 : Top départ à Koupéla Oumarou KONATÉ et Jean-François SOMÉ Minute.bf

items.title: Displaced in South Darfur shelters face critical humanitarian conditions
items.description: The emergency room and health centres in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur, warn of deteriorating humanitarian conditions in several displacement shelters across the city. They say the basic needs of hundreds of families remain inadequately met, amid shortages of food, water, medicines, shelter materials, and hygiene supplies. Nibras Abdullah, a member of Nyala’s emergency room and health centres, says conditions in the shelters have become extremely critical, particularly with the onset of the rainy season. Several families are living in the open or in damaged classrooms whose roofs allow rainwater to leak through, she says. El Jir neighbourhood shelter, which accommodates about 214 families, is facing shortages of food, water, and shelter materials, as well as a need to repair toilets and fit them with doors, empty latrines, and secure the western side of the centre, she says. At El Hamaira shelter in El Wadi neighbourhood, which houses about 274 families, displaced people urgently need food, water, and hygiene supplies, as well as medicines, particularly treatments for chronic conditions such as diabetes and high blood pressure, Abdullah says. El Zahra shelter accommodates about 115 families, while the Mahira School shelter houses about 457 families. Most of the shelters face similar shortages of food, water, hygiene and shelter materials, and medicines, she says. Other centres facing shortages of basic necessities include El Savana, the airport, the commercial school, customs, and the technical school, as well as several other shelters across the city. Families living in the open, overcrowded classrooms Abdullah says some families are still living in the open within the shelters, while others are forced to share overcrowded classrooms, with a single classroom sometimes housing more than seven to 10 families. Several classrooms need roof repairs and doors to provide displaced people with a minimum level of privacy, she says, warning that the rains have made families’ hardship worse by allowing water to seep into their living spaces. Limited support as needs grow Abdullah says some organisations are providing assistance to the shelters, while support is also reaching the emergency room, but describes the scale of aid as inadequate compared with the growing needs. Continually rising prices are making it harder to meet the needs of displaced people, she says, particularly as the available support does not match the increasing number of families living in the shelters. She calls for urgent intervention by humanitarian organisations and the relevant authorities to provide food, water, shelter and hygiene materials, and medicines, as well as to improve temporary accommodation and repair toilets, in order to prevent further humanitarian deterioration as the rainy season continues. items.title: Russie : un jeune homme échappe de peu à l'attaque d'un ours dans les rues de Magadan
items.description: a Magadan, dans l'est de la Russie, un jeune homme a pris la fuite devant un ours qui s'etait aventure dans les rues de la ville. L'incident s'est produit dans la nuit du 24 au 25 août : une camera de surveillance a filme un passant fuyant le predateur, puis l'ours lui-meme est apparu a l'image. Le jeune homme a raconte son experience dans une interview accordee a Ruptly. Homem escapa por pouco de um urso, em Magadan, Rússia. #Russian pic.twitter.com/dUi7d75JEv — Hugo Borges (@hbj_r77032) August 26, 2026 « Je rentrais chez moi, rien ne laissait presager le moindre danger, et voila ce qui est arrive. J'ai reagi rapidement et c'est seulement apres que j'ai compris a quel point la situation etait dangereuse. a ce moment-la, l'adrenaline a pris le dessus, etc. Mais a ce moment-la, je n'ai rien ressenti de tout ca. J'ai simplement compris qu'il fallait m'enfuir », a-t-il declare. Le jeune homme a precise qu'il s'agissait d'« un ourson, pas tres grand », tout en rappelant que « les ours sont deux a trois fois plus forts qu'un homme ». « Il m'a frappe d'une seule patte », a-t-il raconte. Apres l'incident, l'ours n'a jamais ete retrouve, le territoire et les zones avoisinantes etant sous surveillance afin d'empecher qu'il ne reapparaisse. La responsable du departement de la surveillance cynegetique de l'etat, Anna Borissova, a commente l'incident en conseillant de ne pas fuir face aux ours, car ceux-ci sont capables d'atteindre une vitesse d'environ 50 km/h. Selon elle, si l'on se retrouve dans une telle situation, il faut s'eloigner calmement et se mettre a l'abri, puis signaler la presence de l'animal aux autorites competentes. Au cours du mois d'août, les medias russes ont fait etat de plusieurs cas d'attaques d'ours contre des personnes en Russie. Le 19 août, dans la Republique de l'Altaï, un ours s'est introduit dans la tente d'un couple et en a tire une jeune femme de 29 ans, qu'il a dechiree. Le meme jour, dans la region de Kemerovo, au centre de la Russie, un autre predateur s'est jete sur un homme de 50 ans qui rentrait d'une partie de peche. Celui-ci a reussi a s'enfuir. Des attaques ont egalement ete signalees dans d'autres regions de Russie.

items.title: Népal: le bilan des morts monte à 359 personnes
items.description: La crue gigantesque et dévastatrice survenue mercredi dans le nord du Népal, à la frontière avec la Chine, a causé la mort d'au moins 359 personnes, selon un nouveau bilan de la police népalaise. Les autorités chinoises ont pour leur part fait état de 3 morts sur leur territoire du Tibet, portant le bilan provisoire total de la catastrophe à au moins 362 morts et plus de 1.300 disparus. D'une violence exceptionnelle, la crue a balayé la vallée de la rivière Trishuli dans le district de Nuwakot, au nord de Katmandou, et celle de la Bhotekoshi à l'est de la capitale. Selon l'Institut d'études géologiques des Etats-Unis (USGS), la catastrophe aurait été provoquée par l'effondrement d'un glacier, dont la puissance aurait déclenché un séisme de magnitude 5,2, suivi de glissements de terrain. Vingt-quatre heures après la catastrophe, les autorités népalaises restent toujours sans nouvelles de 823 personnes, selon l’autorité chargée des situations d’urgence. Parmi elles figurent 517 ressortissants étrangers. Le bureau du tourisme népalais a notamment recensé 178 Indiens, ainsi que des citoyens britanniques, malaisiens, australiens, néerlandais, américains, portugais, sud-africains, coréens et ukrainiens. L’armée a indiqué, de son côté, que ses hélicoptères avaient permis d’évacuer 105 personnes et d’acheminer du matériel médical et de l’aide humanitaire d’urgence. Un premier rapport technique publié jeudi par le gouvernement népalais a mis en garde contre le risque d’une nouvelle coulée, un lac formé à la suite de l’avalanche n’ayant pas encore été totalement libéré. La possibilité d’une nouvelle vague ne peut ainsi être « immédiatement écartée », selon le rapport. De l’autre côté de la frontière, les autorités chinoises ont fait état de trois morts et de 558 personnes toujours portées disparues, dont 260 étrangers, après le passage de torrents de boue ayant enseveli la zone de Gyirong Port, au Tibet. Un porte-parole du ministère chinois des Affaires étrangères, Lin Jian, a par ailleurs indiqué qu’une centaine de ressortissants chinois étaient portés disparus côté népalais Les inondations et glissements de terrain sont fréquents pendant la mousson, qui s’étend généralement de juin à septembre au Népal et dans plusieurs régions d’Asie du Sud. Selon les scientifiques, le changement climatique contribue à accroître l’intensité et la fréquence de ces phénomènes météorologiques extrêmes. The post Népal: le bilan des morts monte à 359 personnes appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Le Vice-Premier ministre du Royaume de la Belgique chez le chef de la diplomatie burkinabè
items.description: (Ouagadougou, le 26 août 2026) Le Vice-Premier ministre, ministre des Affaires étrangères, des Affaires européennes et de la Coopération au Développement du Royaume de Belgique, SEM Maxime PRÉVOT est arrivé dans l'après-midi du 26 août 2026 à Ouagadougou. Accueilli par le ministre des Affaires étrangères le Camarade Karamoko Jean Marie TRAORE, l'autorité belge est au pays des Hommes intègres pour une visite d’amitié et de travail de 72 heures. L'accueil à l'aéroport international de Ouagadougou a été suivi d'une audience entre les deux hommes, en compagnie de leurs proches collaborateurs au ministère des Affaires étrangères. Les échanges ont permis de mettre en exergue le dynamisme et la qualité de la coopération bilatérale entre le Burkina Faso et le Royaume de Belgique, une coopération établie depuis plus de 50 ans et qui s’opère principalement à travers l’Agence belge de développement (Enabel). Selon le Vice-Premier ministre, ministre des Affaires étrangères, des Affaires européennes et de la Coopération au Développement du Royaume de Belgique, sa visite s'inscrit dans une démarche de renforcement de la coopération entre son pays et le Burkina Faso, dans un esprit de maturité, d'humilité et de sincérité. « Notre volonté c'est de continuer la coopération, pas la conditionner. A travers cette visite, nous avons opté de venir à la source pour écouter et faire des recoupements avec ce qui se dit dans les bureaux à Bruxelles ou à travers les rapports », a souligné SEM Maxime PRÉVOT à l'entame des échanges. Cette approche de l'autorité belge a été saluée à juste titre par le ministre des Affaires étrangères burkinabè, qui a saisi l'occasion pour faire un exposé clair et détaillé sur le contexte de l'installation de la crise sécuritaire au Burkina Faso et l'engagement des autorités actuelles pour y faire face, grâce à une dynamique endogène et à la collaboration avec des partenaires sincères. « Il y'a véritablement la nécessité d'un changement de lecture sur nos pays, et cela passe par l'écoute et le dialogue avec les acteurs qui sont concernés. C'est pourquoi nous accueillons très positivement cette visite, qui vous permettra d'être au parfum de la situation réelle au Burkina Faso », a indiqué le Camarade ministre des Affaires étrangères à son hôte. D'autres sujets en lien avec la dynamique de la Confédération AES et les perspectives de la coopération entre le Burkina Faso et l'Union Européenne dont la capitale belge abrite le siège, ont également meublé les échanges entre SEM Maxime PRÉVOT et le Chef de la diplomatie burkinabè. Au terme des échanges, le Vice-Premier ministre, ministre des Affaires étrangères, des Affaires européennes et de la Coopération au Développement du Royaume de Belgique, dit être édifié et a indiqué que son pays reste engagé à investir « au Burkina Faso, avec le Burkina Faso, mais pas à la place du Burkina Faso ». C'est ainsi la preuve que les relations diplomatiques entre les deux pays demeurent marquées par le respect de la souveraineté, des positions et des choix stratégiques de chaque partie, ainsi que par la sincérité et la transparence dans le dialogue. La coopération entre le Burkina Faso et le Royaume de Belgique s'étend sur de nombreux secteurs prioritaires tels que le développement économique, l'agriculture, l'environnement, la santé, l'éducation, l'entreprenariat, ainsi que la coopération décentralisée, culturelle et inter-universitaire. La réorganisation en cours de la couverture diplomatique belge dans le monde, marquée par la fermeture de plusieurs missions, n’a pas affecté l’Ambassade de Belgique à Ouagadougou. Les autorités belges envisagent au contraire d’en faire un hub consulaire dans la sous-région. La visite d'amitié et de travail du Vice-Premier ministre, ministre des Affaires étrangères, des Affaires européennes et de la Coopération au Développement du Royaume de Belgique au Burkina Faso, sera également marquée par d'autres audiences avec des autorités burkinabè et des sorties terrain. DCRP/MAE L’article Le Vice-Premier ministre du Royaume de la Belgique chez le chef de la diplomatie burkinabè est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Sudan: Kassala gold traders’ strike to continue ‘until street-vendor crisis resolved’
items.description: The head of the goldsmiths’ association in Kassala, Abboud Ahmed Issa, tells Radio Dabanga that gold traders will continue the strike that began on Monday until the relevant authorities intervene and find a lasting solution to the problem of itinerant gold sellers. Issa says the association has repeatedly called on the police, prosecutors, and security agencies to address what he describes as improper practices by some itinerant vendors. Traders are not seeking to bypass the authorities, he stresses, but are asking them to fulfil their role in regulating the market and preventing violations. Among the problems facing the market are fraud, theft, and practices that harm both customers and the reputation of the gold trade, he says. Customers affected by such practices often turn to the goldsmiths’ association after a problem occurs, even though the transaction has been carried out with an itinerant vendor who has no permanent shop where they can be traced. A trader operating from an established shop can be held accountable and required to resolve any mistake or complaint, Issa says. It is much harder to track down itinerant vendors after a sale has been completed, leaving the association to deal with the consequences of problems in which it had no involvement. The phenomenon has been continuing since the Covid-19 pandemic, Issa says, adding that it has worsened in recent years and become a source of frustration for traders, while also damaging the reputation of the city’s gold market. He hopes the government and security authorities will respond to the gold traders’ demands and move urgently to resolve the problem. The association, he says, is ready to co-operate with any arrangements introduced by the relevant authorities to regulate the market and protect both customers and traders. Issa stresses that the strike will continue until a clear solution is reached. Gold traders do not want practices that harm customers or create tensions within the market to continue, he says. Gold traders in Kassala have kept their shops closed since Monday in protest at repeated incidents and confrontations involving itinerant gold sellers, and what they describe as the failure of the authorities to address complaints they have been raising for some time. The closure follows an incident in the vicinity of the market on Monday that escalated into clashes and assaults, leaving one passer-by injured. Traders say it is not the first incident of its kind. According to previous accounts from traders to Radio Dabanga, the spread of itinerant gold sellers outside established shops has created an unregulated parallel market. This has involved, they say, practices including manipulating the weight or number of pieces, and offering prices above the prevailing market rate to attract sellers. Traders have also complained about quantities of gold being traded without official invoices. They say this distorts prices and affects shop owners, who bear the costs of taxes, zakat, mineral and local-authority fees, stamp duties, and security for the market complex. They are calling on the authorities to regulate the buying and selling of gold outside established shops, prevent unregulated practices, and provide protection for the market and those working in it. Editor’s note: This article has been translated from Arabic with the assistance of artificial intelligence, and subsequently reviewed and adapted by a human editor before publication. items.title: Bill Gates on the Dangers of AI
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Bill Gates has generally been an AI optimist. In 2023, the co-founder of Microsoft warned about the potential downsides of AI but in much the same way that a doctor might about a routine-surgery risk—real and serious but, as he put it then, “manageable.” This week, Gates wrote a new memo , headlined: “The Turbulent AI Era Is Here. The Choices We Make Now Are Critical.” This was several shades darker, worrying about economic upheaval, social unrest, cyberattacks, bioterrorism—and most important, the failure of experts and governments to take these threats seriously enough. “The lack of dialogue with all parts of society is kind of deafening silence,” he said in an interview on Radio Atlantic . Gates is still excited about the possibilities of AI. But his new warning emphasizes that what’s coming is like nothing he’s seen in his many decades of watching technological innovation. “Anyone who analogizes AI as a technology to other technologies is missing that this time is different. And saying something is different, there’s a very high bar for that, but I’m staking whatever reputation I have [on] saying this time is different.” Gates joined Radio Atlantic for a conversation about his evolving views on AI, what he misjudged in his interactions with Jeffrey Epstein, and why he’s decided to raise the alarm now. The following is a transcript of the episode: Bill Gates: You cannot expect an industry to regulate itself. That doesn’t work. Hanna Rosin: I’m Hanna Rosin. This is Radio Atlantic . [ Music ] Rosin: In his long career, Bill Gates has been largely a booster of technology—including AI. Very recently, he seemed concerned with the risks but more an optimist on balance. But now he’s written a memo arguing that the combination of the rapid speed of advancement and the lack of regulation is putting us in a dangerous place—for employment and human relationships, and also more immediate dangers, like bioweapons and cyberattacks, which Gates is alarmed that no official entity seems to be guarding against. Bill Gates and I talk about what he is seeing and not seeing around AI, and we talk about what exactly he regrets about his interactions with Jeffrey Epstein. Here’s our conversation. So you’ve been an advocate for technology as a force for good. I certainly think of you that way. It’s Microsoft, your foundation, which rewards innovation. And even when you wrote about AI a couple of years ago, you seemed to be more emphasizing the exciting possibilities and calling the risks manageable. And I would say this week you wrote about AI in a way that’s slightly less sanguine than that. What changed for you? Gates: Yeah, I’m very concerned that we’re not getting a lot of people in the conversation about how to minimize the negative things and, at the same time, how to accelerate the good things. The reason that my tone has changed is that starting late last year, as the models—particularly Claude at first, but now many of the models were very good at coding—their capabilities just keep advancing. And so we’re crossing the danger thresholds in areas like cyberattacks and bioterrorism, and as the reliability goes up, the challenge in the jobs market or even the, you know, psychosocial dependency, these concerns are very strong with today’s models. And yet the response I’ve seen from outside the industry—including policy makers, but you know, even academia or society as a whole—to really debate and look at what we have today, which is, you know, a discussion about voluntary review, but it’s pretty empty where you have no criteria of what level you’re looking for and then what remediation you’d ask for. You know, even common-sense things, like monitoring the use of models that can make dangerous molecules for bioterror, that’s not even been put in place. And yet years ago, we said when we got to these thresholds, we needed government to do that. Rosin: So it sounds like even you were surprised by the—what? By the speed of advancements, or by the slowness of response to the advancements, or both of those things? Gates: Both very, very strongly. You know, the coding is the thing that I was obsessed with trying to do super well from age 13 to 23. And so late last year, where the models start to be as good or in some cases better than humans at coding, that was a real threshold for me. But then even more recently, as the Gates Foundation is using these tools to look at making new vaccines and drugs and things, we see how powerful they are. And we even see in the cyber case models, sort of, what you might term “being out of control” in a surprising way, because the reinforcement learning incents them to succeed, even if you know it means breaking through barriers or conspiring with each other. So people who don’t look at that and go, Wow, we have a serious problem here, but where is the nonindustry activity to set those criteria and debate these things? , my memo has some suggestions on taxes or human-reserved or restricting the level that kids use it to replace real-world friends. But that’s really there to start a broad discussion—not because I’m saying if you just apply what I’m suggesting, then it’s all taken care of. Rosin: Yeah, it sounds like, I mean, in the 50 years of Microsoft, there’s been a lot of disruption—the internet, social media particularly—but not necessarily cataclysmic. Do you feel like AI is a different scale of thing? Gates: Yeah, I wouldn’t use the word cataclysmic, because it’s also wonderful. It’s eventually, it provides medical advice and personalized learning and levels of invention unheard of. But anyone who analogizes AI as a technology to other technologies is missing that this time is different. And saying something is different, there’s a very high bar for that, but I’m staking whatever reputation I have [on] saying this time is different, that something that exceeds human cognition—not just in one area, like farming or mathematics, but across the board, and then in a few years’ time will be coupled with fairly low-cost, quite capable, humanoid robotics—that is a more profound change to our economy and jobs than anything in my lifetime by a dramatic amount. And so the past is kind of there to fool you if you think this technology is similar to other ones, some of which I had the privilege to be involved with—the, you know, microprocessor, personal computer, internet. And even though you have to be careful with those a bit, overwhelmingly, those were good technologies, and overwhelmingly, that led to net job creation. Rosin: Can you get as specific as you can, but still stay realistic, about what worries you? What scenarios you’ve talked to people about or seen as being very possible that we should be all more aware of? Gates: Well, let me take kind of a grim one, which is bioterrorism. You know, I wrote a book called How to Avoid the Next Pandemic , and pandemics can emerge in two different ways. One is intentionally caused by humans, either governments or nongovernments, and that’s what we call bioterrorism, or it can come through just something coming from animals into humans, like a very powerful flu has many times in the past. And now these tools make it so a nonstate actor, a nongovernment, particularly if you combine various tools, will be able to do extremely dangerous things. And I know very well that the quality of these models by the end of this year will be dramatically better than they are today. And so, you know, I’m kind of in a state of shock that the notion that the ability to make molecules—you know, we’re not talking about monitoring that. And you can still have free models, but you have to keep them in a place where they are monitored. And I think every country, including the U.S. and China, should agree that this is beneficial. And I don’t see that as a meaningful slowdown to the innovation in the industry or, you know, letting them figure out how to get the good stuff, which the Gates Foundation is very involved in the education, health, and agricultural pieces there. Rosin: I wanna ask you about some other dangers you write about, like employment and education. But first, you must know a lot of the people who are working on AI. Why do you think that we, whoever the “we” is, don’t think enough about what are obvious dangers? Gates: Well, you know, they’re obvious if you’ve lived thinking about AI as this wild thing your entire life, like I have and some of the people in the industry [have]. I think there’s a great failure to really involve nonindustry participants. If you really look back at what some of the key industry people have said, I give them a lot of credit for speaking out. And it’s not just Dario Amodei. If you take Sam Altman and other OpenAI people, even Elon Musk, who I talked to the least of all these AI leaders, they’re not hiding the fact that they’re concerned. In fact, if you go to the origin story of OpenAI, it was designed with certain safeguards, but those safeguards would only work if there was just one AI company. You know, DeepMind talked to Google management about having some safeguards for their technology. But we have to deal with these challenges at a time when there’s many U.S. companies at the frontier and many Chinese companies at the frontier. And that means that just a company doing something unilaterally is no longer like those safeguards weren’t discussed. That no longer has any effect. And so the lack of dialogue with all parts of society is kind of deafening silence. And, you know, if you don’t anticipate these problems, you could have such a backlash that extreme measures, like Shut it off or something like that, might become politically popular. And yet I still think we can thread the challenge so that we don’t have to slow down, and yet we minimize the bad and have net a lot of good. Rosin: We’re already seeing that with data centers, that it’s just becoming an overwhelming kind of no. Employment is another one I want to ask you about. That is an immediate fear. I remember you once wrote that you didn’t think the labor disruption would be as profound as other periods in history. As the disruption is getting closer, are you more concerned about that? Gates: Well, yeah, I am extremely concerned about the labor-market effects, you know, within the next two years in the white-collar space and within the next four years in both the blue- and white-collar space. Just going back to the data-center thing, I’m afraid that people who think, Okay, we got our local data center not to go through , may feel like, Okay, we stopped AI . That’s not the case. These data centers, whether they show up outside the United States or in some state that’s not as negative, or that the economic reward that the companies offer of local employment and taxes and, you know, making sure that the way they’re doing water and noise and not raising electricity bills is good. So I don’t think that outlet—that’s like saying, Okay, we stopped one pipeline, and now we’ve solved climate change . It almost takes the energy that should go to What should the tasteful regulations be? and pushes it in a Pyrrhic direction. Rosin: Right. Back to employment. Rosin: So you are very concerned about that. Do you envision a world with more inequality? Like, it’s hard to believe that we’ll suddenly value high-human-touch professions. It’s just hard to see what the future society is, even though people talk about it idealistically. Gates: Well, I put forward a concept that I haven’t seen anywhere before that we should have some job categories that are human-reserved. That is, even if the AI, with or without robots, can do child care, you know, should we not allow that? And there’s a lot of things that that would be good, either where you’re allowing the people in that profession to continue to be paid until retirement, or where in the long run you’re saying—in terms of human uniqueness and humans engaging with each other, and just the incredible value of jobs that go way beyond the economics—to not have this disruption. There are a lot of jobs that the only thing holding AI back from taking is that organizing the systems to achieve extreme reliability has been difficult. And I see, over the next few years, both people who do the implementations and the richness of the models themselves completely eliminating that unreliability barrier. And then when you get a cycle at your competitors doing it, then there’s pressure on you to match their cost structure, even though for society as a whole when you replace that person, the safety net, you know, is already underfunded with high deficits, so it’s not like there’s some reserves set aside at this point that can help out there. Rosin: Although, when you start to get to specifics about what the “we” is and what the interventions should be, like reserve certain jobs or universal basic income, it feels almost incompatible with the way that we’ve ordered our society or with capitalism. Like, it just feels like it would require a completely different mindset and world that I’m not sure people are ready to get their minds around. Gates: No, we ban child labor. You know, we require professional certificates to do jobs. I agree that preserving the dynamism of the price-discovery system is extremely valuable. You don’t want to go to, Okay, there’s this one central thing that makes all the food . You want people saying, Okay, I have a Thai restaurant; I have an Indian restaurant , and you know, there’s a lot of freedom and innovation that comes out of that. And that’s why my proposals about the tax system shifting away from taxing labor to taxing capital and picking areas where you say, No, the robots are not going to replace all the humans , in some cases for a period of time and in many other cases never, I think that’s a valid debate. And if people think that’s a bad solution, or they don’t see where it should apply, I think that’s interesting, because then I’d be dying to hear from them what is their solution, because jobs are very important for social connection and meaning. And I don’t want one party to be engaged in helping to minimize the challenge of AI; I want both. They might have differing solutions, but I think it should rise to the top of their list. The data-center thing is getting it there but in a very, very narrow way. Rosin: Yeah, I think what people do say is: Then we lose to China . I mean, that’s the way the argument generally goes. Any slowdown, we lose to China—it’s a legitimate argument because you don’t necessarily want China to control the rollout of this technology. Gates: But let’s be careful. Do you think China wants bioterrorism? Do you think China wants cyberattacks? Our lack of a clear view of how we should be careful, and then once we figure that out, yeah, going to them and saying, We’d like you, for the models that are under your control, not to enable these capabilities either . Until you’ve really been serious about those negatives and what the monitoring solution looks like, you can’t invoke China, because all we have is voluntary review with no criteria. Of course, if you go to China and say, Will you also do voluntary criteria with nothing? , then you can come home and say, They’re not willing to do anything . Well, that’s because you’re not doing anything. You’re not proposing anything that would solve the problem. And the vacuum here, which was filled in by complete cheerleaders a little bit, is very scary to me. Rosin : Yeah, yeah. Okay. There are things that are in everyone’s interest if you talk about them that way. I’m going— Gates: To limit the bads. All of these bads appear in every economy. I mean, the Chinese have really banned kids using AI in a lot of ways. And people are reluctant to say, Maybe we should look at what they’re doing and consider those prohibitions . Rosin: By the way, who are the cheerleaders? Gates: Well, the U.S. government in its desire to, you know, say, Okay, we’re ahead , even under the Biden administration, was involved in making it hard for China to get bearish chips. So we made this, you know, geopolitical thing where we were explicitly trying to slow them down. Now, that’s meant that they’ve invested in their own chip capacities, and you have different estimates on how quickly they’ll be able to replace the chip-level capabilities that we blocked them from getting access to. Rosin: And the heads of the companies, I imagine, too? Gates: Well, I am saying that in my view, these company people are being responsible at speaking out about the challenges of these models. And you cannot expect an industry to regulate itself. That doesn’t work. You have to have somebody who’s mediating and who says, Look, if you don’t get serious about this bioterrorism capability, then yes. If you refuse to put the monitoring in, then yes, you are not licensed to go forward . If you don’t let parents see what their kids are doing, where those friends that they mention don’t happen to be real people— [ Break ] Rosin: I have more AI questions, and we haven’t yet talked about your philanthropy. I’m going to make a quick diversion to the more difficult subject, which is Jeffrey Epstein, because that hangs over a lot of what you do. After the Department of Justice released emails earlier this year, there were a lot of headlines that just put your name together. From what we gather from the public record, you and your foundation staff interacted with him between 2011 and 2014, just in an effort to raise money for global health. And then when you gave testimony to Congress earlier this summer, it sounds like he later learned some things about your personal life, mused in emails about blackmailing you. Is that a fair summary? Gates: Well, he never did blackmail me. This thing is, you know, laid out in complete detail in my full day of congressional testimony, which I was very enthused to have an opportunity where we touched on every meeting we had, every piece of email. But you’re absolutely right—in that January release of emails were things that made it clear he was contemplating working with an associate of mine potentially to blackmail me. He never did. You know, I never paid him anything. I didn’t change the exit package for the employee that he was doing that with. But, you know, it just underscored how foolish I was not to have better judgment, even though my intent was philanthropic. There was never any social thing. I never went to the island. I was never introduced to any women. But I’ve learned a lot from that, and I’m glad that transcript is there so people can know exactly, month by month, what I did do and what I didn’t do. Rosin: You said—you used the word foolish. At the time, you said you knew he had a past sex conviction but didn’t know the details. Looking back, do you have a sense about why you didn’t look into the details? Like, did you make a choice there, I think is what I’m asking, to overlook his reputation in the aim of achieving a certain goal? Gates: Well, he definitely had connections with billionaires, a lot of them. And, you know, in a sense, you could say he found my weak point that by saying he could get tens of billions or 100 billions that would be donated to global-health causes, that raised my interest. And that was enough for me to spend a pretty modest number of hours, but enough that was a huge mistake. You know, he— Rosin: What was the mistake? The mistake was talking to him or overlooking—what do you think of as the actual mistake now? Gates: I thought that him just referring us to people, where I was clear to him he would never get any money, he would never have any role, I thought that the fact that he had this past conviction, which at the time I thought he had, you know, served the time, just like, you know, all sorts of ex-convicts that the foundation works with and trying to get them back into the labor market. I thought the justice system had worked when, many years after I stopped seeing him in 2014, a very impressive reporter in Miami showed that the government justice system had completely failed the victims there. And I was not aware of that. But I did know he’d had that one offense, and he’d served time for it. I didn’t think that just using him as a middleman, that we were so reputationally sensitive that getting literally billions to save lives, that would have been okay. Now I understand the work we do is massively reputationally sensitive, the way we work with governments of all kind and partners of all kinds, and so, you know, I would never take that kind of risk again. And I’ve learned a lesson, and I’ve been able to go through in detail everything that happened. Rosin: The Gates Foundation announced plans to open a regional office in Saudi Arabia. Some people might consider that morally questionable. How do you see that? Is that a similar case of, sort of, you go where the money and the willingness to help is? Gates: Yeah, I mean there are people who buy oil from Saudi Arabia. There’s people who visit Saudi Arabia. We did not engage in the period where the U.S. government was saying, Hey, we’re limiting our connections . We went along with that. But after the leaders in Europe and the U.S. were deeply engaged, I did go to Saudi Arabia and say, Hey, the donors for global health are pulling away, and that’s causing a lot of harm. Would you help me with polio eradication? And they made a, you know, five-year, $500 million commitment to help fund the polio campaign. And they have a relief organization, the King Salman Relief, that does good work in a lot of places around the world. And so, in order to liaise with them and make sure that $500 million is spent well, and the relationships that KSR has that are way more powerful with Muslim countries than we as the Gates Foundation have—yes, we are among the people who visit Saudi Arabia. We don’t buy the oil; that’s, you know, most of the world does that. But yeah, we are trying to help kids not get paralyzed, and our relationship with Saudi Arabia has emerged as a key part of that. Rosin: Let me end with this because I feel someone listening to this might be unsatisfied by one thing. You know, we talk about regulation, government regulation. It feels obviously important and obviously the thing to do. Have you ever sensed that we have the infrastructure to regulate, that we have the willpower to regulate, particularly in this administration? Like, is this a realistic plan? Gates: Well, we have a democracy, and the idea of minimizing harms from unlicensed drugs or, you know, imitating people or fooling old people into spending their money, I still believe the U.S. government has the capacity to help minimize the harms here and even play a leadership role in a constructive way with other countries around the world. You know, I think some would welcome a, Hey, we’re in this together. This is mutual problem-solving, not us taking advantage of you . And so, you know, you’ve got to believe that we all care about this. We’re all, you know, human beings, and now is the time. If I could have picked the time, I would have picked a much later time, but here we are. And the IQ of the society to figure out these trade-offs, it really isn’t engaged. You have graduates who use AI, so they know how powerful it is, and they know that the job market of it shifts; it works against them. So you’re starting to see a little bit of sensitivity in a few areas, but what percentage of economics professors are really looking at this and helping us out with it? You know, I think it’s like 2 percent. And even many of them, when I meet with them, they don’t get that what they are using today is so limited. And so by being in the technology space, and historically I’ve been somebody who said, Hey, the more technology, the better , the fact that now I’m saying, Only if we’re tasteful will we get the goods to outweigh the bads , I’m definitely raising a shrill alarm. I mean, to the level that whenever I do get a chance to meet with world leaders, since 2008, when I switched over to be full-time at the foundation, 90 percent of my message is about helping reduce childhood death rates, where we cut them in half, and we want to do that again during the 19 years left in the foundation. Now the majority of my bandwidth that I get with world leaders will be about AI. And I’m hoping that over the next couple of years, the engagement is so broad and so rich that I can go back to taking whatever time I get and having it again be 90 percent about global health and malaria and polio, not something that brings in my first career experience and, you know, having to be sort of a: You’re not getting it in terms of how profound it is, how much it’s improving, and the incredible efforts gonna be required to restrict these negative effects . Rosin: Did you use the word tasteful ? That was a word I didn’t expect. Why tasteful ? Gates: It’s good? Rosin: Tasteful seems, you know, restrained. Tasteful. Gates: Yeah, well, some of the measures, you know, given the amount of money and, you know, the number of people in IQ, in the history of humankind, there’s never been an area where as much capital or as much total salary where, you know, you have hundreds of companies, even putting aside the robotics, and they’re going full speed ahead, and the idea that the balance of how we require the efforts to go into certain safety things, it’s just not balanced today. And even the industry has said, Well, you know, what are the regulations? Maybe some of those people aren’t sincere. If we come up with these plans, you know, we’ll hear from them. But then again, we’re trying to make this work as a pro-equity factor, for not just the United States but for the entire world. Rosin: So tasteful means more, like, equitable? Less scary. Tasteful is a— Gates: Yes, yeah. No, it’s a tiny bit sarcastic to use such a modest word, given how much is at risk if some of the negative things go unchecked. Rosin: Yeah. Well, Bill, thank you so much for making time to do this today. Gates: Yeah, great to talk to you. Rosin: That’s all for today’s show. [ Music ] Rosin: This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Mike Pesoli and edited by Kevin Townsend. It was engineered and has original music by Rob Smierciak. Claudine Ebied is the executive producer of Atlantic Audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor. If you like what you saw here, new episodes of Radio Atlantic drop every Monday and Thursday. You can subscribe on The Atlantic ’s YouTube page, on Apple or Spotify, or wherever it is you get your podcasts. And if you want to support this work and the work of my colleagues you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener. Until next time, I’m Hanna Rosin.

items.title: Americans Are Spending Luxury Dollars for Dive-Bar Service
items.description: M arcella Patino was hunched over a table at the South Salt Lake Community Center, her pizza getting cold and her nerves fraying. Patino is a single mom with three kids, and kid­like in her own way, tiny and sweet-voiced. When I met her, in the summer of 2024, she was 33 years old and earning $300 a week doing manicures and pedicures. To bump up her income, she had recently gotten a degree from aesthetician school, meaning she could start offering her clients facials and eyebrow lamination too. She would start making $450 a week soon—$23,400 a year, assuming she was able to work year-round with no breaks. Her rent was $1,550 a month. Then she had to pay for electricity, heat, food, clothing, cell service, health care, child care, gas, and everything else. To keep Patino and her children out of abject poverty, the state of Utah was providing her with Medicaid, SNAP (benefits from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, better known as food stamps), and $600 a month in cash assistance. “Is it enough?” I asked. She blushed, picking at her nails, hand-painted with miniature strawberries and lemons. She went to food banks, she said. Her mom and her neighbors pitched in. Still, she kept falling into debt. Whether the help was enough was less of a pressing matter than whether the help would be there at all. A few days earlier, the state of Utah had dropped Patino from its cash-assistance program and SNAP. She didn’t understand why; her caseworker had been no help. That’s why she had come to Circles, a self-empowerment nonprofit that helps its clients boost their income to double the federal poverty line or more. A Circles volunteer, Stephanie Burdick, hugged Patino and logged on to her account at the Utah Department of Workforce Services (DWS) website, as she had done dozens of times over the prior year. She reviewed the notifications Patino had received, read the emails between her and her caseworker, and looked at her pay stubs. “I can’t figure it out,” Burdick said. It was not the first time the pair had been stumped. Her benefits get “turned off all the time,” Patino told me. Because Utah was asking her to substantiate her poverty all the time. Generally, Utahns receiving cash assistance or food stamps have to fully reapply for the programs every six months; for Medicaid, every 12 months. But the state was asking Patino for data on a near-­weekly basis and requiring her to reenroll in each program every month or two. She did not own a computer and struggled to use the DWS website on her cellphone, meaning she would have to go to the library, attend a Circles meeting, or call Burdick for help. “It takes me hours,” she said. “Sometimes, if I submit an application to one program, it messes up the whole entire other set. Then I have to go back and fix all of it.” Paperwork abounded, and errors did too. Early in 2024, the salon where Patino had been working closed down. She was unemployed for two weeks before finding another gig. When she filed the requisite forms, Utah logged her as having two jobs at once and removed her from the Medicaid rolls. Patino found out when she was in the ER. Even her caseworker seemed to be struggling to keep up. At one appointment, he admitted that she had lost her cash assistance because “he didn’t put all the paperwork in.” Her kids vulnerable, her employers exploitative, her bills past due, her gas tank empty, her housing unstable, her benefits unreliable, Patino was emotionally fried. She was startling awake in the middle of the night to check her DWS account. She was afraid to check out at the grocery store, worried that her EBT card would not go through. She was bracing for the gut punch of eviction as she scrubbed the calluses off other women’s feet. And she was spending countless hours dealing with the state—a part-time job, as she described it. [ Annie Lowrey: America’s annoyance economy is growing ] More Americans are getting signed up for this sort of government work, whether they like it or not. Last year, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) created a nationwide work requirement for Medicaid and expanded existing work requirements for SNAP. The policies are “not some onerous, burdensome thing,” House Speaker Mike Johnson argued , promising they were designed to weed frauds and cheats out of the safety net. But the policies are an onerous, burdensome thing—that is exactly what they are. Four million more American adults will have to log their hours to get help with their groceries, along with the 4 million already doing so. As of January, 19 million will have to demonstrate that they are working, in training, or volunteering in exchange for health coverage. Assuming the new paperwork takes the average person two hours a month to complete—a lowball guess—President Trump and congressional Republicans are demanding 552 million hours of work a year from the country’s most vulnerable. The labor would be worth $21 billion at prevailing wages. It would be a full-time job for 265,384 employees. Plenty of people won’t put in the hours and will lose benefits. Plenty of people won’t do their paperwork correctly and will end up churning on and off of programs, or getting handed additional forms to fill out—like Patino. As the Circles meeting got going, I asked Patino how many times Utah had dropped her from one program or another. “Oh, I don’t know,” she responded. She huddled with Burdick for a minute or two. “Maybe a hundred times,” Burdick said, matter-of-fact. “Marcella, you’ve lost your benefits a hundred times ?” I responded. She gave me a what-can-you-do shrug and a half smile. P atino’s situation might be unfortunate, but it is not aberrant or even particularly rare. In my nearly two decades of reporting, I have met homeless people who could not get aid, because they had lost their driver’s license during an encampment sweep. Workers who could not get health coverage, because they were itinerant, constantly crossing state lines. Sick or injured people unable to access disability insurance, because they could not prove they were disabled. That is what you get when you provide benefits the way the United States does: by discretion, with skepticism, through a perplexing variety of programs with a surfeit of fussy rules. The country does not simply approve benefits for those who qualify. It sets arcane standards, creates arduous enrollment processes, and imposes exacting criteria on desperate individuals. In effect, it charges a fee for access to the safety net, payable in aggravation and frustration and effort and hours. I call it the time tax . Americans live in the wealthiest and most technologically advanced society the planet has ever known. They supply $8 trillion to the government each year, employing half a million elected officials, 2 million federal bureaucrats, and more than 4 million contractors. And they spend luxury dollars for dive-bar service. This article has been adapted from Lowrey’s new book . Estonians are automatically registered to vote and can do so online, a process that takes perhaps two minutes. Americans have to register of their own volition, and many then take time off from work to wait in line to cast their ballots, because elections are held on nonholiday Tuesdays. The majority of Japanese citizens do not have to file an income-tax return, whereas the average American taxpayer spends 12 hours on the 1040 and $290 on private tax-preparation services every year. Residents of Taiwan do not deal with insurer-specific provider networks, open enrollment, or prior authorizations for routine care. Working Americans spend half a billion hours a year on the phone with representatives from their health plan. Why stop there? More than half of prison admissions for probation violations are due to technical infractions, such as failing to make a court payment on time. Every year, 11,000 Americans die waiting on a disability-insurance determination, and 5 percent of applicants submit more than 1,000 pages of medical paperwork to government bureaucrats. In the early months of the coronavirus pandemic, Wisconsin answered just 0.5 percent of the 41 million calls made to its jobless-insurance program. Half of workers with a flexible spending account (FSA) fail to spend all of the money in it each year, because FSAs are an inane, time-consuming blight. If a worker does not buy enough contact solution by the plan deadline, their employer gets to keep the money left in the account—diverted from the worker’s paychecks. The American time tax might be ubiquitous, yet it is hardly equally distributed. Non­citizens handle more paperwork than the native-born. People with a criminal record handle more paperwork than those without. The sick face more friction than the well. And poor single mothers such as Patino deal with way more administrative burdens than the pinstriped apparatchiks who passed the OBBBA. When a person needs help, the first challenge they face lies in figuring out what is out there. Washington sponsors more than 100 anti-poverty programs, nearly all of which are aimed at specific needs and many of which are targeted at specific populations. States, cities, and tribes administer most federal schemes, and offer their own, multiplying the multiplicity. As a result, the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF), better known as welfare, goes by at least 32 names: Successful Families, in Kansas; Reach Up, in Vermont; the Family Employment Program, in Utah, though Patino called it just “financial.” I asked her whether she meant welfare. “It is financial,” she said, “when you’re looking for better employment, and they help you for a while.” There’s generally no cross-enrollment among and no common application for these atomized initiatives, because they are managed by different offices at different levels of government, and they have their own rules and standards. SNAP accepts adults whose gross monthly income falls below 130 percent of the federal poverty line, and Medicaid, 138 percent of the federal poverty line. In New York, TANF uses a “standard of need” related to the local cost of living. In Hawaii, the yardstick is 185 percent of the 2006 poverty line. Go ahead and try to calculate that in your head. Applicants have to prove their eligibility on websites that look like they survived the GeoCities era or on overlong paper forms composed in impenetrable High Bureaucratese. The forms can be intimidating: Many states command qualifiers to read hundreds of boldfaced words on the peril of defrauding the government, for instance. They can be confusing: A state might ask a person to detail how they split the cost of staples such as rice with their roommates. They can be pointedly humiliating: Until recently, Michigan asked unmarried pregnant people what day and where their unborn children were conceived . (Obstetricians don’t ask that!) If an applicant makes it through this gantlet, maintaining a benefit is often as difficult as procuring it in the first place. Every year, one in five SNAP households and one in 10 Medicaid recipients “churns” off of and on the program. Patino told me that she once lost her welfare benefits because she had missed a shift or two to stay home with her sick kindergartner instead of going out to apply gels. One time, Utah’s DWS sent her an email threatening to cancel her health plan if she did not send in proof that her oldest child was enrolled in school. Participants have no choice but to try to comply with such demands, fearing retaliation for filing complaints. Burdick wanted to help Patino get back on public assistance, and she wanted to stop DWS from kicking Patino off so often. After the Circles meeting, she went to visit Marsha Judkins, a member of Utah’s House of Representatives, and invited me along. A staunch Republican, Judkins believes in limited government. But she also believes that if a program is enshrined in law and funded with taxpayer dollars, the government should administer it with competent professionalism. Many of Judkins’s constituents had fallen victim to the state’s incompetence, including members of her own family. Not long before, she told me, her son-in-law had lost his job and tried to enroll in Medicaid. “It was a mess,” Judkins said. “My son-in-law cut his head open and had to go to one of his neighbors, who’s a doctor, to get it stitched up because they did not have insurance.” Her voice tight with anger, she described calling the state’s Medicaid administrator to sort it out. “I can call,” she said. “I did. And I got it taken care of. Guess what? They’re on Medicaid the next day. Problem solved! But no, the problem is not solved, because I cannot call for every single person.” After listening to Patino’s story, she decided to help. She tapped out a stern email to the DWS chief: “These delays, mistakes, repeated filling out of forms, wait times, etc. affects the clients’ physical and mental health, which in turn affects their ability to work and function. And how frustrating for DWS workers to not see improved outcomes and success for their clients.” She asked him for ongoing updates on her fellow Utahn’s case. F or a decade leading up to the passage of OBBBA, Donald Trump vowed not to cut Medicaid. As Congress prepared to pass his bill, he reiterated that promise. Changes would reduce “fraud, waste, and abuse” by stopping services for “people that aren’t supposed to be there, people that are noncitizens.” Yet the OBBBA does not merely cull people who were never supposed to be on public assistance from the rolls. It foists paperwork on older Americans, veterans, homeless people, and former foster youths seeking food stamps. It foists paperwork on nearly every able-bodied, childless, working-age adult in the Medicaid program. Already, more than 3.5 million Americans have lost nutrition support. As many as 10 million people are expected to lose insurance coverage in the coming years. I went back to Salt Lake City this summer to see Patino and Burdick, and watch the crisis unfold. One in six participants in SNAP had disappeared from the rolls in a matter of months. “Marginal” households with small allotments were dropping out instead of doing the paperwork, Gina Cornia, the director of the nonprofit Utahns Against Hunger, told me. But seniors and young children were going uncovered too, a change she found ominous and could not explain. At the state’s food pantries, donations were down, and demand was up. The Crossroads Urban Center, a food bank, was “the busiest we’ve ever been,” Bill Tibbitts, its deputy director, told me. “It’s really concerning that we are seeing so many people during a time when the unemployment rate is very low.” Half of the center’s clients were homeless, meaning many of them had just been tasked with filling out a time sheet to keep their EBT card on. A few had asked to comply with the new rules by volunteering at Crossroads after getting something to eat. “If they are showing up as much as they have to for the work requirement, that means they have less time for finding other employment,” Tibbitts said. State capitols were struggling with the changes too. The OBBBA penalizes states with improper-payment rates above 6 percent, forcing them to cover part of the cost of their SNAP enrollees’ benefits. (The improper-payment rate has nothing to do with fraud and everything to do with programmatic complexity and state capacity. Fussy policies, janky websites, heavy paperwork flows, and unreadable forms create ample chances for enrollees and civil servants to make good-faith errors.) Thus, they are increasing verification checks and upping the number of fraud investigations. Some states won’t be able to lower their improper-payment rate below the threshold, and could end the program instead. At the same time, short-staffed and tight-budgeted state offices were spending hundreds of millions of dollars to set up the requisite Medicaid systems by January. Utah was doing so while figuring out how to fill a $200 million Medicaid budget gap. “It is a complicated and complex program, and its complexity has expanded,” Tracy Gruber, the state commissioner of health and human services, told Salt Lake City’s Fox 13 . Many Medicaid enrollees don’t even know they’re going to have to comply with a work requirement soon. Adam Cohen is the CEO of Odyssey House, a nonprofit providing care for people with psychiatric conditions and substance-use disorders. Its patients are “not informed about what is going to be cut, and how to keep their benefits, how to exempt themselves,” he told me. What would happen if his clients lost coverage? They were indigent, he said. They would keep living on the streets without treatment. They’d go cold turkey in jail. Some would die. Odyssey’s clients are among the lowest-income and highest-need in the state. But healthier, better-resourced Utahns are going to struggle with the Medicaid rules too. In 2018, Arkansas briefly imposed a work requirement in its public health-insurance program. Within seven months, one in four enrollees subject to the rules had lost coverage—generally because they didn’t fill out the paperwork. Analysts expect the same to happen with the OBBBA: For every one person who loses coverage because they can’t or won’t work or volunteer 80 hours a month, several others will lose coverage because they can’t prove that they’re working, volunteering, or exempt. And people who can prove it—well, they’ll just be proving it. Work requirements in Medicaid do not change employment rates. They don’t motivate people to work. Nobody expects them to do so now. A ll this, for what? I kept thinking as I walked around Salt Lake City last month. Politicians argue that work requirements and strict enrollment criteria improve programmatic integrity. They stamp out fraud. They discourage welfare dependency. They spur people to get their act together, to work for benefits if they cannot or will not work for a job. Of course, rules and forms and checks can do all of those things. Yet politicians overrate the benefits without even acknowledging the costs imposed on individuals, nonprofits, and the government itself. I used to think that administrative burdens might be the price we have to pay to have a safety net at all. Americans hold an abiding belief that poverty is a problem for individuals to solve, an ideology developed on prairie homesteads, transatlantic steamships, covered wagons, as well as on sharecropper plantations and in segregated stores. Racial diversity reduces social trust, gins up opposition to redistribution, and heightens concerns about fraud. It generates support for time taxes . Still, Americans did not suddenly fall in love with welfare after President Bill Clinton made the program much more punitive in 1996. I can’t imagine Medicaid and SNAP’s public-approval ratings climbing as a result of the OBBBA. And some new evidence suggests that administrative burdens sour people on the government whether they have to comply with them or not . [ Philip K. Howard: Americans are afraid of authority ] The surest thing they do is the most obvious thing they do: strip people of time, energy, stamina, self-esteem, and cognitive bandwidth. A few weeks ago, Burdick, Patino, and I met up at a pizza place in Salt Lake City. Patino bounced in wearing a pair of black scrubs, a uniform from the salon where she works. She beamed as she told me about the good changes in her life: her oldest kid enlisting in the Army, going camping with her younger children, dating a great new guy. “Do you like the job you have now?” I asked. “Are things financially more stable?” “For sure,” she said. “I’m leveling out. I’m doing my best. I haven’t got one eviction notice this whole year, and so that has been amazing.” The stability seemed to have eased her anxiety and given her space to think long-range. She had come up with an idea for a gel-manicure-curing device. “I went to the University of Utah, because they do help for entrepreneurs,” she said. “I’m going to get it patented, trademarked, and I found somebody who will make it and manufacture it here in the U.S.” In the meantime, she was making extra money training new aestheticians. How much had Judkins getting involved helped? I asked. Was she finding it easier to deal with the state? The intervention did make a difference, she told me. For a few months, DWS had asked her for fewer documents and lengthened her reenrollment periods. But then everything went back to the way it was. She started having to reapply for her benefits over and over again. Although she was more financially stable, she was still strained, living in a one-bedroom with her two kids, forgoing meals from time to time. Plus, her income rising had made budgeting harder, in some ways. “I started working at this salon,” she said, gesturing to the black scrubs, “then I started making too much money, and they cut me down on food stamps to $100, and then I had to pay $200 for day care.” She had to make sure she didn’t work too much or else she would lose her insurance. The next day, the three of us went to a Circles meeting, and Patino explained why she was so afraid of losing her Medicaid. She had torn her ACL, making it hard to do pedicures and leaving her in constant pain. Her new mentor, a volunteer and benefits salesperson named Josh Nelson, talked her through it. “If you are making too much money, it will mess up” your other benefits, he said. “Maybe when you teach a trainee, you can say, Listen, pay me when the student graduates .” Then he pivoted: Did she have someone to drive her to and from the hospital? (He’d be happy to do it.) Would she have plenty of healthy meals in the freezer? (He and his wife would love to help.) Did she know where she would get the procedure done? (He could research physicians for her.) Like Burdick, Nelson was trying to reduce Patino’s administrative burden. He was also treating her like a human being. Toward the end of the meeting, Patino told me that soon, she would be not only a client of Circles, but a volunteer. She knew how to deal with the time tax. She wanted to help other moms deal with it too. This article has been adapted from Annie Lowrey’s new book, The Time Tax: How the Government Wastes Our Time—and How to Fix It .

Audience papale : les pèlerins sénégalais reçus par le Saint-Père à la Basilique Saint-Pierre
items.description: C'est dans une ambiance à la fois joviale et solennelle que les pèlerins de justice et paix ont été reçus à la Basilique Saint-Pierre par le Pape Léon XIV. Les larmes, les soupirs et murmures ont été les sentiments les mieux partagés à l'audience papale qui s'est tenue à la Basilique Saint-Pierre du Vatican. Le Pape Léon XIV a été accueilli par des liesses de joie par les différents pèlerins qui se sont donné rendez-vous dans le siège de la papauté. Tous vêtus du même tissu, drapeau du Sénégal en main, les pèlerins de justice et de paix ont fait vibrer la salle à l’entrée du Saint-Père dans la Basilique Saint-Pierre. Certains, les larmes presque aux yeux, n’arrivaient pas à contenir leur joie en posant leurs yeux pour la première fois sur le Saint-Père. Le Pape Léon XIV, après son entrée spectaculaire, a rejoint son siège où il a salué et béni tous les pèlerins ayant foulé la terre de Rome pour le pèlerinage, particulièrement les pèlerins de justice et de paix. Jean-Christophe Diouf exprime sa joie après avoir rencontré le Saint-Père. A lire aussi : Pèlerinage aux lieux saints de la chrétienté: Les pèlerins de Justice et de Paix ont gravi l’Escalier Saint à genoux « La joie ne peut pas être plus grande que celle que j’ai ressentie aujourd’hui quand j’ai vu le Pape franchir la porte de la Basilique. Je n’ai jamais pensé pouvoir vivre ce moment car je ne voyais ça qu’à la télévision. Dieu soit loué, je suis aux anges », s’extasie le pèlerin Jean Christophe Diouf. À la fin de l'audience, les pèlerins de justice et de paix se sont rendus à Assise, à plus de 200 km de Rome. Dans la cité de Saint-François-d'Assise, les pèlerins de justice ont assisté à la messe présidée par Monseigneur Augustin Simmel Ndiaye, évêque de Saint-Louis. Prenant la parole, l'Abbé Martial Goram Mbaye a, dans son homélie, rappelé aux pèlerins de justice et paix la mission du chrétien qui est d'être au service des autres comme Saint-François qui, pourtant issu d'un milieu aisé, a tout laissé pour être au service des pauvres. L'Abbé Martial Goram Mbaye a aussi incité les pèlerins à plus de solidarité, surtout en ce temps de pèlerinage aux lieux saints de la chrétienté. Marie Bernadette SENE (Envoyée spéciale)

items.title: Retraites : François Hollande propose 63 ans et ne ferme pas la porte à une candidature en 2027
items.description: Francois Hollande revient sur le devant de la scene a huit mois de la presidentielle. Dans Unir. Nouveau monde, nouvelle gauche , a paraître le 3 septembre, et dans un entretien au Point , il detaille ses propositions sur les retraites tout en laissant ouverte la question d' une candidature en 2027 apres des sondages flatteurs au debut de l'ete . Âge legal a 63 ans et effort partage « Le dossier des retraites reviendra ineluctablement sur la table », ecrit l'ancien chef de l'etat. Il propose de fixer l'âge legal « aux alentours de 63 ans » au 1er janvier 2028, a rebours de la volonte socialiste de revenir a 62 ans. Puis d'allonger progressivement la duree de cotisation « au fur et a mesure de l'evolution de l'esperance de vie », via « un mecanisme d'ajustement a la main des partenaires sociaux ». Il veut aussi « limiter a 1 % pendant cinq ans l'indexation des pensions », un gain equivalent selon lui au report d'un an de l'âge de depart, et « ajouter une part de capitalisation » controlee par les partenaires sociaux. Les bouleversements du monde mettent nos démocraties à l’épreuve. Tout change. Rien ne sera plus comme avant, mais tout est encore possible à condition de nous unir sur l’essentiel. La France a les capacités de relever les défis qui l’attendent. Les dettes climatiques et… pic.twitter.com/inx3mrsfwR — François Hollande (@fhollande) August 26, 2026 Une position qui tranche avec son combat contre le passage a 64 ans sous la presidence d'Emmanuel Macron. Sur X, le compte SeniorActu a resume : « Francois Hollande avait combattu la retraite a 64 ans : il propose desormais 63 ans en 2028 et cinq ans d'indexation limitee a 1 % sur votre pension ». François Hollande avait combattu la retraite à 64 ans : il propose désormais 63 ans en 2028 et cinq ans d'indexation limitée à 1 % sur votre pension https://t.co/U3xFcCK5BI #SeniorActu pic.twitter.com/Kjz0ldSfza — SENIORACTU.COM (@senioractu) August 27, 2026 Pour rapprocher le salaire net du brut, Hollande propose une baisse des cotisations salariales, financee par « une contribution qui toucherait une partie des grosses successions » et une hausse progressive du taux normal de TVA de 20 % a 24 %. Le taux reduit sur l'energie et les produits de premiere necessite passerait, lui, de 5,5 % a 0 %. Sur une eventuelle candidature, l'ancien president a precise qu'il tranchera en decembre . « Si la situation l'exige et que j'ai la conviction […] qu'un rassemblement est possible et que je peux en etre l'expression, j'en tirerai les conclusions ». Il refuse en revanche de participer a la primaire socialiste d'octobre, estimant que « la plus grande urgence n'est plus simplement de rassembler les socialistes, ou la gauche, mais d'unir les Francais ».
